subsubtopic: SPECIAL EMPLOYMENT INITIATIVES PROGRAM-APPLICATIONS NOT ACKNOWLEDGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament I am accustomed to making representations on behalf of my constituents in order that they may take full advantage of government programs, especially job-creation funds.
I also appreciate receiving courteous treatment by Ministers of the Crown. I regret to say, however, that my efforts to secure funding for deserving projects under the Special Employment Initiatives Program have not been well received. In fact I have sent in many requests for various projects and have not even received a reply.
I recognize that the Minister was a busy man in his quest for the Liberal Party leadership. But I understand that matter has been taken care of and we have a new temporary Prime Minister. Would the Minister now see to it that I receive an answer to my queries? A yes or a no would be sufficient. I do not mind being refused; however, I resent being ignored. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King), has had the same type of problem. Perhaps the Minister will see to it that the dust is brushed off our files and acknowledgements are sent to us post-haste, to show his good faith.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not often that an opposition Member makes a statement which is complimentary to a Crown corporation such as Canada Post, but today I should like to take this opportunity, on behalf of my constituents and millions of descendants of the United Empire Loyalists across Canada, to pay tribute and show our appreciation to Canada Post for issuing a beautiful United Empire Loyalist stamp.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE ON ISSUANCE OF UNITED EMPIRE LOYALISTS COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE ON ISSUANCE OF UNITED EMPIRE LOYALISTS COMMEMORATIVE STAMP
speechtext:
I should also like to express appreciation to all those responsible for their approval to launch this bicentennial stamp on July 3, 1984, in the historic Township of Adolphustown, which is on the Bay of Quinte, the site 200 years ago of the landing of Major Peter Van Alstine and his party of Loyalists. This was also the boyhood home of Canada's first Prime Minister.
It is most fitting that this commemorative stamp be issued from Adolphustown, as on July 17 Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II will officially open the Loyalist Parkway which runs through this, the smallest township of Ontario.
Despite its size, Adolphustown is recognized as one of the most important settlements in what was called the Midland District and is now part of eastern Ontario. The settlement of Adolphustown has played a major role in the history of Ontario as well as of Canada. Therefore, it is most fitting that this Loyalist stamp be launched from Adolphustown.

Mr. Speaker, every Canadian citizen and every permanent resident may, if he or she is residing in Canada and is at least 18 years of age, sponsor an application for landing made by one relative regardless of age or relationship to him or her, where he or she does not have a spouse, child, parent, grandparent, brother, sister, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece who is a Canadian citizen, who is a permanent resident, or whose application for landing he may otherwise sponsor.
The problem occurs when the Canadian resident wishes to sponsor a younger member of the family, such as a brother or sister, niece or nephew. If the Canadian resident has a parent or grandparent still living, he or she is advised that the elderly relative may be sponsored but not the latter.
This is an unreasonable condition in that elderly parents or grandparents are not always in a position to emigrate to Canada due to age, health, or attachment to familiar surroundings. This condition of the Act denies the Canadian resident the right to have a close family member join him or her in Canada, resulting in emotional stress and hardship in many cases.

June 27, 1984
I have some constituents near retirement age who are in need of companionship and emotional support from family members, and who have been good citizens, yet are denied the comfort they deserve in their later years. While the Department of Employment and Immigration is sensitive to family reunification, it is my hope that the Minister will review present legislation and make amendments to this legislation to give these Canadians compassionate consideration.

subsubtopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE DOOR-TO-DOOR DELIVERY IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an urgent need to expand door-to-door postal service to many growing communities across Canada, but Canada Post has not conducted a survey to establish qualification for door-to-door delivery since 1975. Communities in my riding, including Sooke and Ladysmith, have, according to Canada Post standards, qualified for this service since 1976. Saanich also qualifies and has not received door-to-door service.
I understand there has been a directive to cut 73 person-years from Vancouver Island and Powell River postal staff by the end of 1985. This will mean that communities which presently have service may have it reduced, and those which have qualified for almost a decade will not be given consideration. It will also increase the already high and unacceptable unemployment level. This directive must be rescinded and, in addition, a survey must be conducted so that there can be equality among the various communities in this region of British Columbia in the receipt of postal service.

FAREWELL MESSAGE BY MEMBER FOR BEAUHARNOIS-SALABERRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I have decided not to run in the event a general election is called and also because the House is adjourning for the summer at the end of this week and on Thursday I shall be travelling with the Minister of Veterans Affairs to Charlottetown, I want to take this opportunity to say goodbye to all my colleagues in the House.
Mr. Speaker, after twenty-two years in Parliament, I think my decision is certainly justified, but I want everyone to know that it is as hard to leave as it is to enter politics. One becomes very attached to the task of serving the people and to the duties of an elected representative, which include sitting in this Chamber and watching history being made every day. There
are also the friendships that develop between colleagues and transcend differences of opinion, political parties and ideologies.
Mr. Speaker, I too have developed a great fondness for Parliament and this House where, for nine years, I was one of those who sat in the Chair, and where for five of those years I was Deputy Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I personally want to thank you and your predecessors for the consideration you have always shown me.
I want to thank the entire staff of the House with whom I have had an excellent working relationship and whose services were many.
Finally, a special word of thanks to all my colleagues for the spirit of kinship we shared. I want to thank the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Official Opposition, the Leader of the NDP and their predecessors, and also the Member for Yellowhead.
The best of luck to the new Leader of the Liberal Party and future Prime Minister of Canada.
My best wishes to all, my dear friends, and until we meet again.

The purpose of the campaign is to promote Canadian products and urge Canadians to buy products manufactured here in Canada at competitive prices. The launching was attended by the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Retailers Association, many businessmen and people from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, who said they were very pleased to be taking part in this campaign to promote Canadian products. This initiative by the Government of Canada is certainly something to be pleased about, and Canadians should be urged to think Canadian whenever purchasing products for their own use. The slogan "Think about it, think Canadian" is well suited, Mr. Speaker, to the present Government of Canada, and I am sure that Canadians will also think about it at the next election . .. and think about the Liberal Party of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to address an area of concern to me which affects the tourist industry in Canada. The tourist industry is a rather seasonally based industry which is affected by many factors. To have a successful year, tourism must rely on weather conditions. Being actively involved in the tourist industry on Prince
Edward Island during the summer months, I certainly know the importance of good weather to the industry. Our particular tourist industry on Prince Edward Island relies on good summertime weather to encourage tourists to come to the area. In light of this, I would like to discuss the importance of weather forecasting to the tourist industry.
[DOT] (MIS)
There must be more emphasis placed on sunshine. I realize that weather forecasters must project the weather as it exists, but I cannot help but feel that there has always been an emphasis placed on the negative aspects of weather conditions. Emphasis should be placed on the positive aspects of the weather, such as the percentage of sunshine in a forecast.
Weather forecasters seem to deal with determining the negative factors of the weather. The probability of precipitation is determined, rather than the amount of possible sunshine for the day. For example, a broadcaster will say that there is a 10 per cent chance of rain, rather than a 90 per cent chance of sunshine. I feel that visitors to Canada would, either consciously or subconsciously, be more encouraged to travel to various locations in Canada by hearing the percentage of sunshine forecast, rather than the percentage of rain forecast. I feel very strongly that our weather forecasters should emphasize the positive rather than the negative.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Will the Minister of Finance tell the House what he intends to do to offset the unemployment effects of increasing interest rates? If the Minister does not act now, then he is forcing this Parliament to leave here and leave behind it 1.5 million Canadians without jobs, and without hope.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATES ON UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to use the Opposition's own argument, including the argument of the Hon. Member's own dear friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West, who likes to refer very often to the United States, to indicate to my friend that the fact that we have higher interest rates at a particular time, or increasing interest rates, does not necessarily mean that we have higher unemployment taking place. Look at the United States, to use the argument of the Hon. Member for St. John's West, where it has not occurred automatically. On the contrary. The decision of investors, in particular, depends on many factors, not only on whether there is an increase in interest rates but also on whether there is going to be a demand for their products, whether they are going to have greater productivity from their workers, and whether their export capabilities are going to be favourable. The Hon. Member knows that. The best evidence of this is the latest survey carried out by Statistics Canada compared to last October.
Last October the large businesses in this country had foreseen a decline in investment in real terms by 3 per cent. In May they foresaw an increase in real terms by 2 per cent. That was a change of 5 per cent in real terms over and above inflation during that period, even though interest rates in May were higher than they were in October. Therefore there is no automatic relationship.
I do not like interest rates to go up. I regret that they have increased in the last several months. We have done and are continuing to do everything we can to keep that increase at the minimum possible level, and this is going to continue to be our policy.

subtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
EFFECT OF INCREASED MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister knows, obviously, from his response to the questions just asked, that the interest rate issue is perhaps the most serious question confronting the Canadian economy. The Minister also knows, I am sure, that as a result of last week's increases in the bank rate, the five-year mortgage rate has risen to 15 per cent from 12.5 per cent in January. This puts housing out of the reach of another 100,000 Canadians. It means that a person who renews a $75,000 mortgage over five years will have to pay $8,000 more today than that same person would have had to pay in January. It means that the housing starts which were predicted at 170,000 at the beginning of the year will not reach 135,000, and we are going to have 75,000 more people out of work.
Given that the Bank of England has now stated categorically that it cannot follow the U.S. lead in interest rates and it will establish an independent policy in Britain, why is it that the Canadian Government cannot do likewise on behalf of Canadians?

subtopic: EFFECT OF INCREASED MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to five-year rates because he prefers to choose the highest possible rate. He knows that if you want a three-year or one-year mortgage you will get a lower rate than the ones he mentioned. He must realize that there are some choices in the market for interest rates you are ready to pay and the risk you are ready to take. He also knows that in the last several days this House passed, thank God, a mortgage rate protection plan. This will ensure some protection for borrowers who want to buy a house against future increases in interest rates in years to come.
As to the specific point raised by the Hon. Member, I will study with interest the position of the Bank of England. But I must remind him that some European countries tried a similar approach a while ago and they had to reverse their position completely, 180 degrees. They ended up having to pay a very, very high cost indeed. I only have to remind him of the experience of socialist France which tried a similar approach of going it alone at a particular time. They had to pay a tremendous economic price for the policy choice they made. They had to reverse course completely a year later, and they are still paying for it.

Mr. Speaker, I do not understand how the Minister can evaluate an economic price and draw the conclusion that those unemployed will not have to pay a tremendous economic price for the policies of this Government, or that those people who will not be able to renew their mortgages will not have to pay a tremendous economic price as a result of the policies of the Government.
The Minister knows full well that since 1981 interest rate increases have resulted in over 500,000 jobs being lost, and 30,000 businesses, along with 80,000 individuals, going bankrupt. There are now over a million more people in poverty in Canada than there were in 1981. Given that, how can the Minister stand in his place and say that he is prepared to support Gerald Bouey's insane high interest rate policy at the expense of the lives of Canadian families?

The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain is good at rhetoric, but he is not so good at analyzing the facts. I may remind him that the point is not whether we can do our own thing and ignore the rest of the world in which we live. The Hon. Member was quoting figures on unemployment in Canada. I may remind him that in France, for instance, after following a direction that differed from that followed by the rest of the industrialized world, at a given time, they finally created a situation where, unless I am mistaken, the French franc has decreased in value by about 90 per cent over the last two years. I may also remind him that the present unemployment rate in France is higher, not lower, than it was two years ago. It has gone up. So the point is not whether unemployment is too high today, or whether interest rates are too high. I realize the unemployment rate is too high. I realize that interest rates should be lower. I am doing everything I can to bring these rates down to the lowest possible level. However, I shall certainly not adopt policies that will result in more unemployment and in devaluating our currency, which happened in a number of European countries as a result of pursuing policies that appeared to be expedient in the short term but soon proved disastrous. I shall certainly not take the lead of the New Democratic Party in this instance.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. This month another batch of students are out on the streets looking for jobs that do not exist. Many of them will be living off their families, or lining up at food banks. What does the Minister intend to do about this intolerable situation? Is this the Liberal election platform for youth?

Mr. Speaker, last week when we released our report, Focus on Youth, we realized that there was indeed unemployment at the rate of 18.5 per cent and that this does not include those who are not looking for jobs and would need to be trained. In the last Budget of the Minister of Finance, $150 million was set aside, and $30 million is now going to be devoted to a youth training option which I feel is certainly a beginning to finding a solution for those people who are unskilled and have a hard time finding a job.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance. It concerns economic policy. By adopting a "jobs first" policy the NDP Government in Manitoba has reduced youth unemployment from 21 per cent to 10 per cent in one year, while the unemployment rate has gone up in other provinces, as the Minister knows. Why does the federal Government not adopt a similar kind of economic policy and put jobs first as a national priority? Why is this happening only in Manitoba? There have been a number of provincial Governments which have taken some initiatives. Some have taken more than others. He said: Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members are aware, the motion before the House would have the effect of saying that women or men who have three months of continuous employment with the same employer would be eligible for the maternity leave and child care provisions as set out in the Act. This would mean that women and their husbands could choose after three months whether or not they wished to take maternity
June 27, 1984

leave or child care leave. It would affect those women who come under the protection of the Canada Labour Code.
My motion, in effect, is the proposition which was introduced to the Minister when he tabled the Bill in the House in May. What has happened over the last week is that, in collusion with the Conservative Party, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) backed down in committee from the promise he made to women across the country, to people who wanted the child care provisions to apply after three months. By moving to a six-month qualifying period many women, many parents throughout this land, will not qualify for the leave.
I will give an example of how this would operate. In committee we had representations from the Canadian Construction Association. They did not want the present law, which provides for maternity leave after 12 months' continuous employment, changed. In my questioning of the representatives of the Canadian Construction Association, they admitted that most of their tradespeople only had three or four months' employment with any one employer. What the provision which the Liberals and Conservatives agreed to in committee will do is this: Women who work in the construction trades will not qualify for maternity leave and neither parent will qualify for the child care provisions. In my amendment I am trying to re-establish what the Minister promised to women and parents across this land when he tabled this Bill. I am trying to undo the harm of the Liberal-Conservative coalition in committee which prevents many women and parents qualifying for this leave.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak briefly to this amendment. We spent a week in committee where we heard many witnesses. The first witness we heard was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet). He assured us that the Bill represented his best judgment as to a compromise between the interests of labour and the interests of employers. At that point I asked whose responsibility it was to protect the interests of society. It is all right to have vested interest groups. I believe it is fair to say that labour is a vested interest group and that employers are a vested interest group. Surely it is the purpose and the place of the House of Commons of Canada and the parliamentarians who serve in this House on behalf of all the people in Canada to have the responsibility and the function of protecting the public good.
As the week unfolded, it became clear that the Bill was not a true compromise between the two vested interest groups. In fact, the Bill as presented to us was clearly a Bill which favoured the vested interests of organized labour. Parts of the Bill favour employees, wherever we find them, but large parts of the Bill dealt with conditions of work that are normally part of the collective bargaining process.
What the Minister of Labour was attempting to do was to take those and, through the legislative process, remove the possibility of collective bargaining. That is something we expect the New Democratic Party to support. I am sure they would support an amendment that said zero months, that there
Canada Labour Code
be absolutely no qualifying period; that for employees under the union banner, those that are captive of the union movement, there would be no qualifying period required. The individual employer would be responsible for the costs associated with it.
The only Party that faithfully attended all the hearings and attempted to serve the public well was the Conservative Party of Canada. We truly tried to find the best kind of labour legislation. You can have a piece of legislation dealing with the necessity for some period of continuous employment to be served before an employee acquires a right, in this case the right to 41 weeks of leave. There is one set of conditions which prevails when society pays the cost of that leave. There is a different set of conditions which prevails when the individual employer must pay the cost of that leave. That is one of the flaws in this piece of legislation, that the Government, the Liberal Party of Canada, in conjunction with the NDP, refused to change the Bill to remove the obligation of an individual employer to provide certain benefits that cost money.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to do that for the House. I am pleased that occasionally we do something unanimously.
The principle to which I was addressing myself was the principle of who pays. The Minister has brought forward a Bill which states that an employer will hire someone who subsequently becomes pregnant. That someone, or the spouse of that someone, is entitled to 41 weeks of leave and the employer is responsible for the benefit costs during that period.
If we are going to require in the laws of Canada that an individual employer pay the benefit costs for someone for a period approaching 41 weeks, the least we can expect is that that person provide some period of continuous service before being entitled to that leave. It was 12 months, 52 weeks. The Government proposed that it be cut to three months or approximately 13 weeks. The committee in its wisdom came to somewhere in between and moved it to a period of 26 or 27 weeks, in effect six months.
I suggest that probably we are still wrong in principle to require the individual employer to carry the cost of that leave. If that period of leave for child care is something that our society values, then I suggest that society in total, through general revenues, some kind of insurance or some other scheme, should pay the direct costs associated with that period of leave. However, the Government was unwilling to so provide.
The Government has supposedly had a change in leadership and a change in direction. It is still a government that is loading a specific cost on to a specific employer that is totally out of the control of that employer. That cost is in the hands of those who seek the leave and if such leave is deemed to be of benefit to society, then it is a cost which should be paid for by society rather than by the individual employer.
Surely, given the fact that the Government insists that the individual employer be responsible for that cost, it is at least reasonable for any employee who is to benefit from that provision to provide the employer with a period of continuous service that is longer than the normal probationary period which attaches to many forms of employment. That is why the committee was virtually unanimous in its decision to amend that provision of the Bill from three months to six months. I would encourage the House to accept the six-month provision. It is not a great provision, it is not a perfect provision, but given the individual responsibility, it is certainly better than the three-month provision.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak very briefly to the amendment to Clause 6, where it refers to Section 59.2 of the Canada Labour Code, proposed by the New Democratic Party. Originally, the Canada Labour Code, as the previous speaker just said, prescribed a period of twelve months, and when Bill C-34 was introduced, this was reduced to three months, more or less as proposed in the amendment by the New Democratic Party.
Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, the groups that testified before the Committee of Labour, Manpower and Immigration, especially those representing management and obviously those representing workers who are all very much in favour of the Bill. In all fairness to the employers, we cannot really say that they are against the Bill but they did use a term, and this term was used by Mr. Masters who is President of or represents a group called Fetco . . . employees who fall under federal jurisdiction and work for a Crown Corporation. He said quite simply to bring in a balanced bill. So, regarding the existing period of twelve months and the three-month period proposed in the Bill, we felt in Committee and also in the Government that to balance the situation and strike a bargain that would be fair to both workers and employers, a period of six months would be entirely reasonable.
June 27, 1984

I was very pleased to hear my hon. friend from the Progressive Conservative Party say that he wanted the period to be set at six months. I know that on their side, they supported the amendment I proposed on behalf of the Government, which meant that all employees with six months' continuous service shall be entitled to what we provide under Clause 59.2.
Since we were talking about more balanced legislation, in Committee all three Parties tried to deal equitably and fairly with the groups appearing before us. I know that the Progressive Conservative Party was very much in favour of the six-month amendment, and that the Government proposed the six-month amendment since it wanted to expedite this Bill.
As for the three-month proposal, I myself and other Government members believed that going from twelve months to three months was too great a step and that some kind of compromise was preferable. Of course such compromises are necessary whenever a Bill is considered in Committee by the various parties, and I believe that this time we were very successfull, considering both the time element and the number of witnesses that were heard. We were able to reach an agreement among the Parties so that the Bill could be reported back to the House without delay. Mr. Speaker, that is why, if we are talking about balanced legislation, I feel that we should vote against the amendment proposed by the New Democratic Party and that we should proceed with the Bill as amended. I think we should put the question on this Bill unless some of my hon. friends have further comments to make.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will be prepared to have the question put in just a moment. Regarding this particular provision, I think the members of the New Democratic Party are saying that we did not have enough time to deal with this Bill. I believe it is a cry for help. We did not have time for a proper consideration of the Bill or to make better improvements to it.
During the discussion of this particular clause, I for example proposed that there might be some sort of a sliding scale of from three months up to 12 months, and perhaps even have extended benefits on one end or the other. Our real concern is for the formation of families. How does this provision affect mothers and fathers who are bringing children into the world and into their homes? We were concerned, for example, that the provision of 24 weeks and 24 weeks cannot run at the same time or that any part of those weeks cannot run at the same time.
This Bill should have accommodated the fact that a mother goes to the hospital, has a child, brings the child home and that is when she needs the help of the father or husband. Most people cannot afford to take two weeks, three weeks, a month or 41 weeks off work. However, they need that immediate time at home to help get the family started. That is the kind of concern for men, women and children that we were trying to have reflected by an amendment. I feel that if we had had more time, we could have in fact met the needs of individual
Canada Labour Code
families and the needs of the creation of families in a more considerable and appropriate manner.
If that is what is being expressed by the motion moved by the NDP, then I am in support of the idea of expressing concern for inadequate amendments that have been made by the Government. We then came up with a compromise and this compromise will have to stand until a Conservative Government can look at this matter in more detail.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. A few moments ago one of my Conservative colleagues suggested that the main beneficiaries of this legislation and particularly of this clause were organized workers in Canada. He somehow attempted to infer that members of the NDP, as Conservative members often charge, are in the pockets of organized labour. I would simply point out that the main beneficiaries of this provision in the Bill are the workers in Canada who are unorganized and do not have union protection. That is a fact. If anyone would care to study at least 50 per cent of the collective agreements in Canada, and particularly those for the industrial sector and perhaps even more for the public sector, he or she would find that these kinds of benefits are already in existence.
It should also be made very clear that we are not talking about paid maternity leave. We are talking about leave of absence for reasons of maternity. There is a vast world of difference between the two, particularly in terms of the cost. The original Bill that came before the committee contained a provision the same as that contained in this NDP amendment requiring that the employee must have completed three months of continuous service before becoming eligible for this maternity leave. On the initiative of, and after pressure by, Conservative members on that committee who requested that the provision be extended to six months' continuous service in order to qualify for unpaid leave of absence, the Government acceded to that Conservative pressure. What my NDP colleagues and I are attempting to do with this amendment is to restore this particular clause of the Bill to its original form so that after three months of continuous service, a period of time which I and I believe most Canadians would deem as being fair, employees may be entitled to unpaid leave for reasons of maternity and for child care where it is required following birth.
I think the amendment is fair and I think the concept is fair. We have been waiting a long, long time for it. Particularly, Canadians who do not have the benefit of being protected by a collective agreement and by the benefits of union representation have been long awaiting an opportunity to have fair treatment. Unpaid maternity leave is certainly the minimum they should be able to expect and demand of their elected representatives in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to determine whether some of the arguments which were used in committee the other evening might be a little more persuasive in this Chamber today. Hon. Members will recall that the New Democratic Party, in the midst of the time constraints which the Government had placed on the House, chose to keep the Chamber sitting until 5.05 a.m. in the morning for voting purposes. Members will also recall that at 9.30 a.m. that same morning, the committee commenced its hearings once again. That same day we discussed this Bill clause by clause and finished at approximately 1.30 a.m. in the morning.
Members were tired when we reached the proceedings which dealt with possible amendments. It seems to me that the committee did not act with the kind of wisdom which the Chamber has come to expect from committees. Perhaps the Minister, with a good night's sleep under his belt, may have had some occasion to reflect on the instructions which he gave to his voting troops who appeared. They had not heard the
witnesses, but as is customary in this Chamber they came to vote.
The Speaker has grouped these three motions for debate and has indicated that there will be two votes in order to dispose of the three amendments. Motion No. 2 and Motion No. 3 have been grouped together.
The most positive feature-and it is a very, very desirable feature-of this piece of legislation is the degree to which it extends the principles which are important to the preservation of health and safety in the workplace. Human life and health are important to all of us. This Bill is an important step foward in the preservation of human life and health in the workplace. The basic principle of that extension is that today we are legislating workers' rights. We are extending to individual workers, to workers collectively and to health and safety committees, certain rights. In Motion No. 2 and Motion No. 3, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) is proposing the logical extension of that mentality. He is proposing that a right should be accompanied by a responsibility. A right which is not accompanied by a responsibility is not as much of a right as it could be or as it should be.
The amendment reads:
(e) co-operate to the best of his ability, with any person exercising-
That indicates that any individual in the workplace has the responsibility to try to the best of his ability to co-operate with worker health and safety committees. The amendment indicates that individuals have a responsibility to their fellow employees and to the public to try to the best of their ability to co-operate and to put into practice good health and safety measures. There could be the best rules in the world, there could be 20 people in the workplace, and there could be the best health and safety committee, yet if one of those 20 workers refused to co-operate with the health and safety committee, what is the purpose of it?
Those of us who have children have said to them: "Do not touch the stove when it is on. Do not touch the burner. Do not grab the kettle when it is full of boiling water". That is a good safety precaution. However, if the children do not obey those instructions and go ahead and touch the stove or grab the kettle, they will get hurt. Quite often a child might not hurt himself, but the child will hurt his baby brother, baby sister, or best friend with that kettle of boiling water.
That is the little chunk of logic, Mr. Speaker, that is missing in this Bill which the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) spotted. He asks Hon. Members of this Chamber to approve just the simple piece of logic that a right is stronger and more effective when it is accompanied by a responsibility, in this case, the responsibility to co-operate with health and safety committees and officers. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is not too much to ask of the Government. That is what Motion No. 2 and Motion No. 3 which we will dispose of with one vote are asking for. I urge Hon. Members of this Chamber to vote yes in order that we can deal with it in a positive way and enshrine it in this legislation.
June 27, 1984

I really do not know why the Speaker has grouped Motion No. 4 with Motions Nos. 2 and 3 because Motion No. 4 is a very different principle. We are enshrining, Mr. Speaker, in this legislation the rights of individual workers in several ways, the most important of which is the right to refuse to carry out a task which would endanger that worker's life or health. Motion No. 4, Mr. Speaker, extends that right to the unborn child.
If the Minister is going to vote against Motion No. 4,1 wish he would stand in this House and tell us why. In committee, Mr. Speaker, he would not tell us why. He would not speak to it at all. He just shook his head no, and members voted against it. Surely, if Hon. Members of this Chamber are willing to give adults certain rights to protect their own health and safety in the workplace, they should also give the right to those same adults to protect the life, health and safety of the unborn child. Who else will act for the unborn child?
It is a tiny amendment, Mr. Speaker, with significant repercussions. Motion No. 4 simply extends the right which we afford to adults, who are capable of taking care of themselves, to the unborn child, who is not capable of taking care of himself or herself. If Government Members do not want that right for the unborn child, surely one of them at least will have the courage to stand in this Chamber and tell us why he or she believes that the unborn child does not deserve that kind of protection.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative amendments under Motions Nos. 2 and 3, while they appear to have no great substance or purpose other than to allow a discussion on these particular clauses in a general way during debate of this Labour Code Bill, cause me some concern. To most people these amendments would sound reasonable, if they were not acquainted with the reality of the workplace. I quote Clause 83(1) (e) of the legislation with respect to Motion No 2:
While at work, every employee shall (e) co-operate with any person exercising a duty imposed by this Part or any regulations made thereunder;-
And with respect to Motion No. 3, Clause 83(l)(f) reads:
While at work, every employee shall (f) co-operate, with the safety and health committee established for the workplace-
The amendment in motion No. 2 reads:
(e)	co-operate to the best of his ability, with any person excercising-
The amendment in motion No. 3 reads:
(f)	co-operate, to the best of his ability, with the safety and health-
Those amendments sound very reasonable and justified on the surface. However, putting this wording in may have an impact of a nature which causes me some concern. It may force employees to take an unrealistic degree of responsibility for enforcing safety, whereas under every provincial workers' compensation act and regulations, the prime responsibility for enforcing safety properly rests on management because it alone has the right to direct the workforce.
I do agree that an employee has a heavy responsibility for protecting his own life and the life of his fellow employees.
Canada Labour Code
However, the prime responsibility must rest upon those who have the power of management. These amendments would tend to force employees rather than management to take the prime responsibility in enforcing safety, to a far greater degree than it is reasonable to expect them to do without placing their jobs in jeopardy. That is the key point.
I would like to give a couple of illustrations. As chairman of an industrial union safety committee and as secretary of a joint management-labour industrial safety committee in my own place of work, Kootenay Forest Products, now Westar, in Nelson, British Columbia, I had to risk my own job a number of times in order to enforce the laws of that province. I had to do so in defiance of warnings and instructions from my employer. While some of us may be a little more gutsy on occasion, I feel it is a little much to expect an average employee to put his job on the line in order to enforce the laws of the workplace, the contract, the province or the country. Most people will just not do that.
I will give an example of a situation under provincial jurisdiction, but it could happen in some industries under federal jurisdiction. It is contrary to the Workers' Compensation Act and regulations in the Province of British Columbia to walk across a moving conveyor or a moving chain. However, in order to keep production moving, workers do that because, contrary to some mythology, the basic purpose of most employees is to put in a good day's work for a good day's pay. Most employees are very conscientious, so conscientious in fact that they sometimes put their lives at risk. The law is very clear in British Columbia. You do not cross a moving conveyor or a moving green chain, but in order to clear up plug-ups, workers are always following the example of their supervisors and jumping up while the machinery is moving to try to straighten out a jam. They take the chance of injury and sometimes the chance of being killed just to keep the production line moving.
On a number of occasions when I saw a worker going beyond what I thought was reasonable-and I was not rigid on that; there has to be some flexibility because our main job is to keep the production flow going-I would simply shut down the machinery and stop the mill. I did that because I could see that some workers were getting too careless and doing that sort of thing too often without forethought. I was threatened with discipline many times but I was prepared, if necessary, to go before the compensation board, take it to the press and to the public in order to draw attention to the lax enforcement of the safety and health laws of that province. Not every employee is willing to do that.
In other cases, my colleague, who used to rotate with me sometimes between being union plant chairman and chairman of the safety committee, has physically picked up employees by the scruff of the neck and threatened them for doing acts which endangered their fellow workers. He was placing himself in jeopardy in order to co-operate to the best of his ability with the decisions of a safety committee and safety management and the laws of the province. He had physically to threaten people, which is a possible Criminal Code violation, in

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
order to stop some of his fellow workers from threatening the lives of their fellow workers by acting carelessly in order to keep production flowing. These amendments may be with the best of intentions, but that is often the problem.
We have an assembly here which is composed largely of people who do not understand the realities of the real world in heavy, blue collar industry. If you have never done anything more dangerous than stabbing your finger with the end of a paper-clip, you cannot understand the values of and the way things work in the real industrial world. For that reason I think the dual amendment, while I believe it is made in good faith, is a mistake and would compound the problems of safety and health enforcement rather than help alleviate them.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult to understand how Motion No. 4 can be grouped with Motions Nos. 2 and 3. Presumably it is for procedural purposes and we will be voting on them separately in any case. I intend to confine myself to Motion No. 4.
This is an important piece of legislation and we have to be careful that we do not rush it through the House. I did not participate in the committee phase of the Bill, but my colleagues did and I believe had sufficient time to focus attention on a number of serious ways in which this Bill is flawed. One of those flaws is addressed in Motion No. 4.
During my examination of the evidence presented to the committee by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, I was struck by their brief. The chairperson of their employment committee recommended that Clause 85(1 )(a) of the legislation be amended to protect not only the woman operating a video display terminal, but her unborn child.
Before I get into arguments supporting that position, we would do well to remember that VDTs are becoming more and more a part of the workplace, particularly the office workplace. We know from statistics that 80 per cent of workers in the service sector are women. If you narrow that down still further to clerical occupations, the percentage is probably higher. All you have to do is go into any bank in this country to see a dramatic exemplification of that fact. We also know that the service sector will probably be the one most affected in the short term by technological change. We now have the introduction of microchip technology in the office workplace through the use of word processors and various other kinds of computerized equipment which, of course, carry with them video display terminals.
What we do not know is just exactly what is emanating from these VDTs. There is a grey area here that science has yet to identify. There is some evidence to indicate that it does constitute a health hazard both to a woman and to the woman carrying a child. Surely, then, the benefit of the doubt should be given and that situation addressed. The amendment proposed by the NAC seeks to correct that situation, and I quote the chairperson of the NAC:
We would ask that you include a paragraph which would read: Every employer shall, in respect of every workplace controlled by him, provide a 15-minute break to each employee who has completed one hour of work in front of a video display terminal.
She goes on:
The employer shall provide annual eye examinations by an ophthalmologist chosen by the employee for employees who work on video display terminals and the employer shall pay to the employee the equivalent wage that he would have paid had the employee remained on the job for the period of time spent undergoing the examination.
That deals with the impact of VDTs on the eyes, but what concerns me here is the impact of this relatively new source of radiation on the unborn child. We are not dealing with something new or breaking new ground because it was addressed by the task force commissioned by the Department of Labour. One of the recommendations of that task force was that employers accept the following guidelines concerning VDTs. First, that pregnant women have the right to be reassigned to other positions without loss of pay, seniority and benefits. That is pretty straightforward. They were impressed enough by the arguments they had encountered during the course of their investigation to come to that conclusion. To quote from page 53 of the task force's report, which goes back to March, 1982:
-the National Action Committee on the Status of Women brief reminded us that standards of what is "safe" can change, as was the case with asbestos. The argument goes that perhaps old VDTs or inadequately maintained VDTs emit more radiation. Or perhaps some sort of synergism occurs in a worksite comprised of several VDTs that could amount to a hazard?
The following excerpts from the many briefs we received show the quandary we found ourselves in. For instance, the Canadian Air Line Employees' Association stated that at Dorval Airport in February, 1981, seven out of thirteen pregnant VDT operators miscarried. The Hospital Employees' Union, Local 180, British Columbia, told us that out of six pregnant VDT operators, two miscarried and of the four babies carried full term, only one was born normal. The B.C. Federation of Labour reminded that four out of seven pregnant VDT operators in the classified ad department of The Toronto Star gave birth to babies with congenital defects.
That seems to me to be sufficient evidence to give the benefit of the doubt to the protection of the woman carrying an unborn child who is exposed to a VDT.
It seems strange, indeed a bit of a paradox, that this amendment would be moved by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. One of the things that group is well known for is its position on the abortion question. But here they join the argument and have put forward the case for the protection of the unborn child, which I think is rather interesting. It reminds me of the fact that medicine is treating the unborn child as a patient in its own right. Indeed, medical science permits doctors not only to treat the unborn child as a separate patient, distinct from its mother, but in certain instances to perform surgical procedures on the unborn child by removing it from the womb without severing the umbilical cord and, upon completion of the surgical procedures, putting the child back in the mother's womb. Usually that stage of the pregnancy is completed. Medical science recognizes the importance of the protection of the unborn child and the right of the unborn child in terms of medical practice. The law is coming around to that recognition as well.
June 27, 1984

Surely the onus is on us to correct what I consider to be a very serious flaw in this Bill. We must ensure that women are protected from the emissions of VDTs and that pregnant women know that the child they are carrying in the workplace receives this protection also. I believe the problem was addressed quite adequately by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and is summed up in the amendment put forward by my colleague which I commend to the House.

speechtext: The Chair is prepared to recognize the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). 1 doubt that there would be any opposition to his speaking at this time. Nevertheless, I must inquire, since he is the mover of the motion, whether there is unanimous consent to allow the Hon. Member to speak at this time. Agreed?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, through all of these amendments we are trying to send out a signal that the Conservative Party cares about people. We are serious about public health and safety. We are concerned about public health and safety as it relates to new technology. That is not just the technology of a video display terminal. It could relate to other technologies still unspoken of today and still to be found. That is why it is expressed by the word "thing" in the amendment. If these technological developments may bring damage or threat to the mother, who is the worker in this case, or to the unborn child, we should demonstrate care and concern. If we are wrong in this legislation, all we will do is err on the side of caution.
Doctors tell secretaries who are working before video display terminals to be careful. They say that although there may be no proof yet, they should try to stay away from those display terminals because the unborn child may be affected. We want to provide protection and give that kind of insurance.
In these amendments we are setting a tone which recognizes the health and safety of people. People are the basis of our workforce and our whole productivity. They are significant and important. By passing these amendments we indicate those kinds of things. It will be very regrettable if the Government does not accept those motions and the intent of the motions.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) spoke on Motion Nos. 2 and 3. I would like to speak on Motion No. 4 with respect to the rights of female workers. The amendment basically says that she would be able to refuse work if she had reasonable cause to believe that the operation of the machine or the "thing" constituted a danger to her unborn child.
If we do not have this provision in the Bill we run the risk that arbitration in the future will decide that a woman does not have the right to refuse dangerous work if it does not affect her health but only affects the health of her unborn child. I would prefer that we specifically mention the right of a woman
Canada Labour Code
to refuse dangerous work or the operation of a potentially dangerous machine if she has reasonable cause to believe that it could hurt her unborn child.
I believe that if the Minister had spent more time considering this very important amendment he would agree to it. One of the previous speakers mentioned the history of VDTs. Some people on the other side may say that there is no evidence that VDTs do harm. On the other hand, if a woman believes that it is a dangerous situation which is going to be harmful to her unborn child, she should have the right to refuse that work. The same thing can apply in many areas.
I find it ironic that in the past employers have refused to allow women to do certain jobs because they believed it would be harmful to the unborn child. We have allowed that in many situations. An employer can tell a woman that she cannot work on a particular job because it would be dangerous to her unborn child. We should certainly give the mother that same right. I believe all of us in the House can agree to that. I would like to hear a reply from the Minister on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the three amendments.
First, amendment No. 2 and amendment No. 3 which have been grouped for the vote, and then amendment No. 4 which has also been grouped with amendments Nos. 2 and 3 for debate, but which will be voted on separately.
My comments concerning amendment No. 2 and amendment No. 3 are very simple. Indeed, I made those comments when the committee was considering the Bill and I pointed out to my Progressive Conservative colleagues that the amendment they were proposing was redundant in the sense that we already have the expression "due diligence", in Clause 83(1 )(e) of the Bill, which is found in Clause 105(5)(Z>) and, therefore that is was not necessary to have an additional amendment which is nothing more than a repetition of what is already proposed in Clause 83.
I gave the same explanations to the committee, Mr. Speaker, and I should think that there is no need at this stage to repeat in the act what is already in Clause 105.
As to the proposed amendment motion No. 4 which would allow an employee to refuse to work if there is a danger not only to himself or herself and her unborn child, that is indeed a very important question. The Government wants to protect not only the mother and her unborn child but all employees under the Canada Labour Code. The series a of amendments we have proposed to Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, which include a number of important amendments to provide better protection for men and women at their work place, have been the subject of extensive consultations between union representatives and employer groups.
There was no specific recommendation concerning this question submitted by the representatives of either the unions or

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
management. To accept at the very last moment this amendment without any proper consultation with the representatives of management and the unions would not be well received in my opinion. I cannot, at the very last minute, accept such an amendment which could change substantially the rules of the game and create a very important exception to our Labour Code as it was not discussed as thoroughly as it should have been with the representatives of the unions and the employers.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the objectives which the representatives of the Progressive Conservative Party wanted to achieve in moving this amendment will certainly be acknowledged. There is no doubt that, during the discussions which will take place between the representatives on the committees ... In passing, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize that the amendment we are proposing to Part IV of the Code provides for the setting up of committees in the workplace including representatives of both employees and employers to deal with all matters related to work safety. I am convinced that the setting up of these committees under the Act will protect not only mothers, but also unborn children, and that appropriate action will be taken to protect adequately Canadian women in the labour force.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would the Minister entertain a brief question which might be helpful?

Yes, Mr. Speaker.

The Minister encountered Motion No. 4 in committee last Thursday evening. It is six days later. Did the Minister attempt to consult with employers and labour in the intervening six days? Has there been a solid attempt to consult to see whether or not this amendment was acceptable?

Mr. Speaker, for weeks on end all kinds of consultations were held not only by myself but by senior department officials. It has not been felt at this point that the matter should be included in amendments to the Labour Code. I am not saying that eventually, labour market developments will not lead to other amendments along the lines proposed by my hon. friend. But at this point, I contend that such an amendment would be premature, considering there has not been adequate consultation, especially since information on VDTs is not complete, and the studies which were made are not conclusive.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Wenman (Fraser Valley West) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 5
That Bill C-34, be amended in Clause 29, by adding immediately after line 15 at page 48, the following:
"(c) the rationale for the change"
He said: Mr. Speaker, again this is a tonal amendment. It is meant to add a tone of civility to the Labour Code regarding how employers and employees will hopefully react to one another with respect to technological change. The amendment adds the word "rationale". In other words, it asks that reasons

June 27, 1984

be given for the introduction of new technology. We would hope that by bringing those reasons forward technological change could be brought on line in a manner that is co-operative, as opposed to the confrontationalism which presently seems to be the tone of labour-management relations in Canada.
The purpose of this legislation is to instil a new attitude in our concern for women, unborn children and other such concerns. That is why we have added the word "rationale". It is only reasonable that if an employer is going to make changes that could affect the workplace he should explain the reasons for those changes to the employees before the rumours begin.
It is a very concrete motion. I am confident that the Government will accept this motion, in keeping with the spirit in which it is proposed.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to speak in favour of the amendment. It is a particularly minor amendment which I do not believe the Government should have any trouble accepting. I suggest that the very fact that the Conservative Party can propose an amendment which will be an imposition on the employer would indicate that it would be acceptable to most employers across the nation.
If technological change is going to be introduced, as it would come under the auspices of this Bill, certainly employees have a right to know the reasons for implementing those changes which will cost people jobs or affect their job opportunities in the future. If we could hear from the Minister, perhaps he would accept this amendment. I believe it would help the relationship within the workplace.
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, I heard the representations of the two Hon. Members who spoke before me, and I feel this amendment has prima facie merits. I do not think it is improper to ask an employer to tell his employees the reasons for the change when he is attempting to make major technological changes.
Therefore, I am ready to accept the amendment on behalf of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to hear that all three Parties are supporting this amendment. Most Members of this Chamber know that along with Senator Nurgitz I worked for several months this winter developing a report on the issue of technological displacement and manpower training and retraining. I felt disappointment in the Bill concerning the clauses affecting technological change in view of the calibre of the evidence we had before the committee on the issue.
One of the conclusions from those months of investigation about new technology in Canada is that we are more like a Third World nation than a modern nation when it comes to our willingness and commitment to adopt new technologies
Canada Labour Code
which would put us back into a competitive position in world terms. Our failure to adopt new technologies is one of the primary reasons that our economy is in trouble, that our dollar has dropped so dramatically, why our interest rates are so high, why we have two million unemployed people and why Canada has slipped from having the second to having the thirteenth highest standard of living in the world. We do not have the attitudes, the systems, the tax policies and the people necessary to take this country into what I might think of as the 20th century, but certainly the 21st century. It is a crisis that we are facing, Mr. Speaker.
I am pleased this amendment has been accepted by all three Parties. I think it has been sufficiently explained. All it really does is provide that an employer who is introducing a new technology will share with those employees who will be affected by it the reasons for the change.
The biggest problem we are facing when it comes to the introduction of technology is the knowledge problem. We do not have enough Canadians at the management level or at the employee level who know, understand and have a feeling for the new technologies. That was clear from the responses we got to the questions we asked in committee. The most disappointing group of all, in my opinion, was the group representing the Canadian Labour Congress. I think those people had a contribution to make. The sense of panic which their leadership felt about the possibility of the whole Bill failing made them say to us: "We will not help you. We will not testify and we will not put on the public record our best ideas as to how to make this piece of legislation better". They said: "Hold your nose and pass it because we are panic-stricken". I think the Congress sold their members short, this Parliament short, and the Canadian people short with that kind of attitude. Certainly in this area of technological change, the Canadian Labour Congress has put some resources into it, it has some understanding of it, some clear-cut ideas of what needs to be done, and the nation would have been better served if the Congress had put those thoughts on the public record so we could have had better consideration in committee.
I am pleased at this small step we are taking. I wish we could have taken a larger step.
