Mr. Speaker, in rising to debate Bill C-34 at third reading, I must raise some points that I have repeated time and time again in committee. The Government has not allowed adequate time for proper study and representation, nor has it allowed enough time for input. The nature of the amendments which have been received indicates the Bill was inadequately drafted, not completely thought out, and that not enough time and consideration was given to consultation by all three Parties.
When the Minister first came to the House he talked about consultation. I accepted that the Minister and his Department had consulted widely and recently had made his intentions known as to the nature of the legislation, and that he had somehow received general approval. We can see by the Minister's own admission today that new technology, video display terminals for example, simple technology that has been with us not since yesterday but for many years, was a subject that was not really talked about and that there were not really any consultations.
Why was that? Certainly there is concern raised throughout the community about video display terminals. Is it because the Government says that first you have to harm women who are pregnant, that you have to have damage done to unborn children, and then when we can prove children have been damaged and a mother has suffered serious harm, we will consider legislation? Why not consider some legislation in advance? Why not make this an important part of the study? Why was this subject not introduced into the committee, allowing the committee to bring forward a study or to raise awareness in the community about it?
The Minister said he had been consulting for four years. We heard from witnesses that the Minister has not consulted with them for months, even years. We heard from major groups who are affected by this legislation. This makes one wonder about consultation. This point was brought out time and time again in committee. Areas that were not dealt with were pointed out and these included areas of technology, health and safety and issues of concern to women generally.
We are concerned that we did not have sufficient time in committee because the Bill was not introduced sooner, although we did spend hour upon hour upon hour in committee. The House should be aware that, in spite of the late presentation of this Bill, members of this committee worked long and hard. They heard brief after brief after brief. We started hearings early in the morning. We could have started earlier. We wanted to start two weeks ago, but unfortunately we could not because the Government had not introduced the Bill into the House. We could have started then, but even when we started we agreed to start at 9.30 a.m. and kept going every night to almost midnight in most cases. We came to the House of Commons. We sat until six o'clock in the morning, after which time we went home and changed our clothes. We were back at 9.30 a.m. to start the committee hearing again. From 9.30 a.m. until 9.30 p.m. we heard presentations before the committee. We were still sitting at midnight. We were still
sitting at one o'clock or two o'clock in the morning, at which point we adjourned.
We did not have time to read the briefs but just had the briefs presented to us. The presenters did not have time to read them to the committee. As committee members we did not have time even to read the briefs. We were listening and we were busy throughout that time. It was an insult to those who spent even a limited time preparing their representations. They complained that they had only two or three days in which to prepare. To their credit, many of them did a fine job. It was an insult to them that the committee did not have the time to hear them fully or to explore their avenues of concern. It is antidemocratic. It is wrong to do this in a democratic society. It is an abuse of our freedom. It is an abuse of our responsibility. I am disappointed to have been forced to participate in it in that manner.
Most of the shortcomings of the Bill as presented could have been corrected with further consultation, even at committee level. If it had been tabled earlier in the session, it could have been discussed for a more extensive period of time with the parties affected, who would understand its implications. It could have been discussed with Members of Parliament. The Government could have allowed us to have an appropriate amount of time in which to prepare the required research, research which should be at the level of debate and discussion of Members of Parliament. However, because of shortage of time the treatment has been only half a loaf.
Of course, those who were mostly left out tended to be those in employers' groups, the people most directly affected. As I stand here today, I am receiving new telegrams from groups across Canada that only found out this week, having read about it in the newspapers, what was happening. They are writing or telegraphing us saying "Just a minute", yet we in our political expediency are forced to rush the Bill through the House.
When announcing the legislation, the Minister set the whole tone of pressure, hurry and lack of caring. In fact, that is what it represented as far as I could see. Even in the press conference which we attended the Minister referred to extended compulsion. In the committee hearings another Minister used the following words: "We will force them". Where is the necessary element of consultation, co-operation and civility in this attitude of force and confrontation?
The Canadian Bankers' Association, not a great favourite of mine, testified before the committee. They said that to say there has been consultation is a little misleading. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business called the exercise a charade and refused to appear before the committee because it had not been consulted.
The Government and the New Democratic Party did not want the Bill to go to committee. My colleague indicated that he was surprised and disappointed in that the New Democratic Party did not want full consultation. When in fact the Progressive Conservative Party insisted upon hearing the Canadian
June 27, 1984

Labour Congress, business groups and interested parties such as academics, religious groups, women's groups and individuals, they said that it would delay the Bill. They indicated that the Bill would not be as good and that something would happen to it. But we insisted upon the hearings. We insisted upon a democratic process. We indicated that in fact we could meet those provisions, bring the Bill before the House and in fact improve it.
We have improved the Bill. If this Bill is not an improved one, I do not know why all Parties in the House passed unanimous motions supporting changes. Why are amendments being put forward by the New Democratic Party? It has been demonstrated that because the Conservative Party insisted upon full democratic hearing, we had full democratic hearings. We worked very hard, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) and others. In fact, I want to put on the record that the Conservative Party was the party of workers on this Bill. At all times in the committee hearings we had a full complement of members. We were entitled to three members and we had three there. In many cases we had four or five there. That cannot be said by either the Government or the NDP.
We are not entitled to that many.

No, but they are entitled to have one member there. I am sorry to tell the Hon. Member that there were occasions when they did not even have one there. Also I am sorry to tell him that that happened in the labour debate in the House of Commons. It was the only labour debate to have been held in the House of Commons during this Parliament. It was held on a motion of the Conservative Party. During that one brief afternoon there were many occasions when there was not even one New Democratic Party member in the House of Commons.
You did not know what you were talking about.

If we did not know what we were talking about, why did the Hon. Member not rise and say something? He did not rise and say a thing. His Party sat there quietly throughout that debate. We were concerned about this legislation at that time. We tried to get second reading on the floor of the House of Commons. The Government would not bring it forward. Therefore we took one of our Opposition days and brought it forward. We expressed our concern that the Bill was not adequate to meet the concerns of women in the workplace and that it was not adequate to meet the concerns of health and safety. That was our motion. That was the only one debated. The level of participation on the part of the Government and in particular the New Democratic Parly in the corner over here was disappointing.
Not a soul in the world would believe that.

I hear the Hon. Member. If that is so, I would ask the House Leader to obtain the minutes of the committee meetings. He could simply look at the recording of who was present. The world will have to believe it because it is
Canada Labour Code
recorded and it is true. In fact, I have the record somewhere right here. If the Hon. Member does not know how to read through it, I could give him the specific pages and dates. I have them right here. They indicate who was present and who was not present. I am disappointed to say that it is demonstrated by the record that on occasion the New Democratic Party did not even have one representative there to hear the points of view of the groups appearing before the committee. It is too bad, it is a tragedy, but that is the way it is. In fact he will notice in every copy of the minutes that Conservative Members were present. Usually it was a full or better than full complement.
It is partisanship to express that kind of disappointment in the New Democratic Party and, of course, in the Liberal Party, as I have enunciated again and again, over the whole process it has placed upon the Bill. However, there was a very worth-while moment in committee. That moment was when a Conservative motion was put forward which received unanimous consent. The NDP supported the Conservative motion. The Liberal Party supported the Conservative motion. It was a motion of substance and great principle. In fact, it probably discussed one of the greatest principles in the House of Commons. Of course, I am referring to the amendment to the Rand formula for conscientious objectors-the right of individuals in this great society to dissent or to opt out, the very basis of freedom.
Our Leader, the Hon. Member for Central Nova (Mr. Mulroney), spoke about another minority issue in the House of Commons on October 6, 1983. He spoke about the generosity of the spirit typical of Canadian society and said:
Our respect for the rule of law, our unparalleled record in civil liberties, our sense of tolerance, our respect for neighbour and his property have combined to make Canada an admired nation of the world.... The issue before us today is one of simple justice ... the sanctity of minority rights. There is no obligation more compelling and no duty more irresistible in Canada than to ensure that our minorities, linguistic and otherwise, live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice. . . . Mr. Justice Hand referred to it as the "spirit of liberty." He told the group of immigrants that the spirit of liberty is the spirit that is not too sure that it is right. The spirit of liberty seeks to understand the minds of other men and women. The spirit of liberty weights their interest alongside its own without bias. The spirit of liberty knows that not even a sparrow falls to earth unheeded. The spirit of liberty, he said, is the spirit of Him, who near 2,000 years ago taught mankind a lesson that it has never quite learned and never quite forgotten, that there may be a kingdom where the least shall be heard and considered side by side with the greatest.
If I had my choice on this particular part of the amendment, it is that the legislation would have gone much further than the amendment that has been proposed. If I had my personal choice, intellectual conscience would also have been recognized as well as religious conscience. Intellectual conscience is the trinity of body, mind and soul. There are equal and valid reasons for an exemption on the basis of intellectual conscience as there are for religious conscience.
I do, however, realize the great implications if in fact we had gone that far. I realize the great debate it would have caused in the House of Commons, again delaying this legislation. But what a shame that somehow in this House of

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
Commons I so seldom hear debate about freedom, about the rights of individuals, about individual choice, about ultimate democracy, about intellectual choice, the value of intellectual-ism. These lofty debates do not occur enough here. Sometimes we touch these debates just a little bit with an amendment. This is such an amendment. It is worthy of support of all members of a democratic House of Commons such as this.
I am disappointed that the Government did not include it in the Bill. Again, it must have been their hurry. I would be interested to hear the Minister clarify that somehow he is accepting an amendment, certain parts of which he did not like. That really surprised me about this Minister. 1 hope in this debate the Minister will clarify why he did not support religious conscience or why he did not put this in the Bill in the beginning, and why he reluctantly gave his consent as he did. I have reviewed the transcripts. I am going to give him the benefit of the doubt before I carry on further about what he said, but I was very disappointed and surprised that a democrat such as he would have had the reservations that he had regarding this legislation.
In this particular amendment the tenets of faith of the major fundamentalist group who advocated this exemption are in fact the very foundation and value structure upon which this nation of Canada is built. In fact, not just Canada but all western nations have been built and maintained upon the basic tenet, the basic value of religious freedom, freedom of conscience. This faith has carried forth the whole basic value concept of our society, our concept of democracy and the very foundation of our lives and our belief structures.
It is essential that it be recognized that this amendment in fact did, as I said, cross Party lines. It does more than cross Party lines. This amendment is not new in the House of Commons; it has been brought in by political Parties of all persuasions across the country.
I was particularly pleased with the motion. I chose to introduce the motion of the Seventh Day Adventists, which I particularly liked because of the way it sprang from their conviction, and I liked the positive way they presented it to us. In the end, in discussion we felt that because it had been tested in the courts, we would move to another great Conservative jurisdiction and seek the advice of the Government of Ontario. We chose the amendment basically of the Government of Ontario. This is the amendment that was accepted. It states:
Where the Board is satisfied that an employee, because of his religious conviction or beliefs, objects to joining a trade union, or to the paying of regular union dues to a trade union, the Board may order that the provision in a collective agreement
(a)	requiring, as a condition of employment, membership in a trade union, or
(b)	requiring the payment of regular union dues to a trade union,
does not apply to that employee so long as an amount equal to the amount of the regular union dues is paid by the employee, either directly or by way of deduction from his wages, to a registered charity, within the meaning of the Income Tax Act, mutually agreed upon by the employee of the trade union.
Where an employee and the trade union are unable to agree on a registered charity for the purposes of subsection (2), the Board may designate any such charity as the charity to which payments should be made.
In the committee we talked about improving even that particular amendment from the Ontario Conservative Code. We felt maybe there was some way to move it away from the Labour Relations Board, that somehow this could be between the worker, his union and his employer, because the principle is so significant that it could not be a mutual agreement, that we would have to add to the workload of the Board.
I would like to have seen some type of an amendment which could have caused that mutuality, that tone. Maybe in future Parliaments we will have time to do that. Again, even with this amendment we had to reach out and grab what was available. Nothing was prepared by the Department. We had to reach out to other resources where they took time to study and to listen. As I said, I am disappointed that there was not more study done on probably what was the most significant amendment to this Bill.
We tried to do other things with this Bill as well as move that amendment. Some amendments have been successful, some not. In committee, and now as part of the Bill that has been reported back to the House of Commons, the Conservative Party strengthened the provisions that protect workers from sexual harassment through an amendment brought to us by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women.
I pay tribute to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) who worked very hard. After we sat in committee, she met again with the group and they worked on drafting such amendments. To her credit, working with that committee and assisting the committee resulted in amendments such as those the Conservative Party made on behalf of issues of concern to women.
We clarified the definition of sexual harassment as being any conduct, comment, gesture or contact of a sexual nature that might on reasonable grounds be perceived by that employee as placing a condition of a sexual nature on employment or on any opportunity for training or promotion. Before this clarification, the perception of sexual harassment could have been made by any employee, including those not involved. The clarification leaves the perception of sexual harassment of the employee involved. I think that was an appropriate amendment.
The Conservative Party also strengthened the Bill's sections on occupational health and safety. We were concerned about people and the accident rate in Canada. The accident rate causes more work stoppages in Canada than all the strikes put together. That is serious. The workplace needs to have greater concern about health and safety. We did not feel that this Bill was in any way going far enough as far as measures of health and safety are concerned.
One area that we wanted to change was where an employer's duties include the obligation to investigate, record and report to the authorities as prescribed all accidents, occupational diseases and other hazardous occurrences known to the employer. We added the words "known to the employer" in order to clarify that such incidents known to the employer will be his responsibility.
June 27, 1984

Not only were we concerned with the safety of workers in the workplace, but as well we wanted the protection to extend to the general public. To the clause which described the obligation of the employee to "report to the employer any thing or circumstance in a workplace is likely to be hazardous to the safety or health of the employee or any of his fellow employees", we added the phrase "or other persons granted access to the workplace by the employer". In other words, we took what I feel is quite a progressive step.
Through this addition, we have said that we are not only concerned about the health and safety of an employee or employer but we are also concerned about the health and safety of other persons granted access to that workplace. We are concerned with public safety and public safety is as important as individual employer and employee safety. I am very, very pleased that our amendment was accepted by the Government and now forms part of the Bill that is before us today.
The addition of those words broadens the range of persons whose safety should be of concern to employees when reporting accidents or hazards in the workplace. People in the workplace who are not employees now enjoy the same protection as do others. These are just some of the improvements that our Party introduced in committee that have been accepted by the Government. Unfortunately, the Government failed to accept the greater protections for workers which were contained in other amendments made by members of the Progressive Conservative Party in committee. Those amendments were dealt with very quickly. They were amendments upon which even I would have liked to have had more thought, more discussion and more broad consultation.
We wanted to define very clearly what actions an employer could take to punish those guilty of sexual harassment. We suggested that the employer be empowered to take disciplinary measures as outlined in the policy or as provided in the collective agreements. Instead, the Government stuck with its own vague wording: "the employer will take such disciplinary measures as he deems appropriate".
We are concerned about the potential hazards to workers resulting from exposure to video display terminals and we expressed that concern in an amendment. Unfortunately, the Government decided to turn that amendment down. We proposed several amendments other than the one that is before us today relating to new technology and the health dangers that are created thereby. I am disappointed that those amendments did not receive more consideration and that there is not more time to include them in the dicussion here this afternoon. Of course, the Government rejected those amendments on the basis of cost, putting the health and safety of workers secondary to economic considerations.
The most tragic rejection of an amendment was the Government's failure to protect the rights of the unborn. We are still disappointed by that. Just today, we have pleaded with the Government to hear us. The Government has yet to announce that there will be some form of in-depth study done to assure
Canada Labour Code
the protection of our workers from new technology and particularly the technology of video display terminals. Again, there was a principle inherent in this particular amendment. I believe that the Labour Code is important because it deals with principles and is supposed to show the way. I believe that any government legislation that shows the way by going beyond a worker to a child and beyond a child to an unborn child is legislation with a worthy principle. That worthy principle should in fact have been included in this Bill and I am disappointed that it has not been. I am pleased that we have at least taken some time this afternoon to discuss in the House of Commons this particular situation. I am sure it is a situation that a new Conservative Government would wish to address on an early occasion.
Time is passing quickly and we certainly do want to give others an opportunity to speak. I could go on to speak of a great many other things we brought up in committee. Those are on the record of the committee hearings. Of course, we wanted to recognize the contribution made by academics to the creation of this legislation through the presentation of ideas. Therefore, we called for a particular amendment that related to the megaprojects provision in Clause 22 because we felt that there had not been enough empirical study on the implications of "carve-out" agreements.
The Canadian Construction Association presented a 600-page academic study entitled Megaprojects, which was written by Weiler, Hebert and others. That study outlined some of the adverse effects that magaproject carve-out agreements may have. We want to see any legislation that we create somehow add to the stability of the workplace because that is what workers want and that is what our society needs. It is to the mutual interests of all that we should have that stability, that agreement and those sound labour-management relations.
According to this academic study to which I just referred, the intention to create such an attitude may in fact create the opposite. It would appear to us that this study was not looked at adequately before this matter was brought forward. The representations of Mr. Weiler included concerns regarding too much ministerial power being granted in determining what constitutes a major project. We suggested that this should be defined in the Code and qualified only if necessary to the public interest. There was also a fear that short-term major project contracts with high wages could cause instability and work stoppage in general construction projects by drawing workers away. However, I would put on the record of the House of Commons that the Minister did make a promise. I hope he will make that same promise here today. He made a commitment to have further consultations and make further studies regarding this megaprojects provision. He spoke about the method by which this particular clause of the Bill may be proclaimed in order to ensure that there would be no disruption.
On behalf of the Dominion Marine Association and the Canadian Lake Carriers Association, we also moved to exempt the shipping industry from Part IV of the Code because of the jurisdictional overlap that could occur with the Canada Ship-

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
ping Act and the Canadian steamship Act. We did not secure that provision but the Minister has assured us that full consideration of the legal implications will be undertaken before royal assent. We will hold him to that, although we may be looking to a new Minister by the time we get around to that process.
In committee on May 15, after my prompting and questioning, the Minister made the following promise:
I think that indeed it would be very useful that there be public hearings and that the number of union and employers' representatives be invited as witnesses to give views on the legislation and possibly to suggest amendments to improve the legislation one way or another. I would think that it would be very useful. I would look forward to it and indeed I would not oppose it. 1 think 1 would encourage such a thing to take place.
The fact that the Minister did encourage and allow such consultations to take place is a tribute to the Minister, even if it did take him 43 hours to do so. I believe we got two hours' sleep out of 43 or 45 hours at that time. However, I did wish to recognize and appreciate the fact that this has gone through the democratic process and, as we complete the Bill today, it is still going through the democratic process and will have full process of law. The only thing that did not follow the full process was the fact that there was not as much time as there should have been for members of the public to understand the Bill before they made presentations. Timing was the greatest villain, and in this case it was the responsibility of the Government.
I could carry on, Mr. Speaker, but as I look at the clock and in view of the time, I would like to demonstrate to members of the New Democratic Party something we demonstrated in committee. One of the members of the New Democratic Party said in debate that if the Conservative members proposed it, it must be all right because employers listen to Conservative members. I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we have demonstrated that we did listen. We heard not only from employers but from union groups, women's groups and academic groups. We listened to as many of the individuals and groups as we could. We even heard from religious groups. We called for and heard from a cross-section of the Canadian public and that is who we represent. We do not represent only the workers. We do not represent only the employers. We represent all groups. We are not bound or tied to anything except the interests of the public and the broad public will. The only interests we represented in every case were the interests of a broad cross-section of representatives. We spoke fairly-
Just like Bill Bennett.

I am sorry that the Hon. Member who just spoke did not attend the committee hearings. We made amendments on behalf of all of these groups. We were their spokesmen in committee. We protected their right to be heard. Once they were heard, we presented amendments on their behalf for discussion. Many of those amendments were accepted.
Hopefully, the Conservative Party has signalled to Canadians that it is open to hearing and willing to working in a manner of co-operation, open-mindedness and civility. We want to end the tone of confrontation which has been featured in Canada far too long. We will be a government of reason which will be open to all groups and representative of the broadest cross-section of our society.
I thank the House for the opportunity to speak on this subject. I look forward to an opportunity in the fall when we can begin to study these appropriate and important issues in more detail.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? On debate, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say at the outset that I listened with great attention to the contributions made by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) on third reading of this legislation. I was very impressed by his remarks, as I was by his performance in committee, which as he stated was of a marathon proportion. He worked together with his colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who has a particular interest in human relations. I think the Conservative Party has been more than co-operative in the passage of this Bill. I do believe that the contribution made by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) meant that the committee consisted of Members from all Parties and had common objectives.
The first objective was to pass the Bill on time because of its admitted advantages. Some of the changes were obvious and were required for the benefit of workers. Second, I think we felt an obligation to produce what has been described as the balanced Bill. Unless labour Bills are balanced to the optimum, they can hardly be effective.
I would like to speak very briefly about a number of matters on which the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West spoke- technological change, safety and women in the workforce. I do so, if not with expertise, at least with concern for these particular issues.
I arrived here in 1962. It might have been before the Hon. Member was born, although I am not sure. My maiden speech in the House of Commons was about industrial relations, although I was an employer of labour at the time. Later on, I had the privilege of being the Minister of Labour who brought in the first modernized Labour Code. In order to signify the progress which has been made in the last 15 or so years, that Labour Code reflected the findings of what I had recommended to students in the industrial relations field. The Woods task force was established. It was a multimillion dollar study performed by academics and experts over the better part of two years. That study reflected the terrible labour unrest of the sixties, when technology was brought very much to the fore and the Labour Code of the day made it virtually impossible
June 27, 1984

for workers to have any input into the impact, whether negative or positive, of technology.
Indeed, I remember in the early 1960s when the railway workers of western Canada lay down on the railway tracks in Wainwright and Nakina in order to make their point. Because collective agreements were of fixed durations-and under no circumstances could they be re-opened for negotiation-management would astutely introduce amendments which dealt with technology or technological change in the middle of a contract. The most flagrant example of that was the introduction of diesels which replaced steam engines. That made it possible for the railways to by-pass the beautiful little communities of the west which were entirely dependent on the trains stopping for coal. Virtually, those communities were wiped out by the new technology. The railway officials had a very good case. They said that they could not reject technology any more than a cotton gin, the Industrial Revolution or the wheel. We were determined to bring in a labour code which made it imperative for management to consult and then negotiate with the workers, not whether technology should be introduced, but that the impact be minimized if it was negative and that the rewards be shared if the impact was positive.
I must congratulate the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet). He has brought in a Bill which, as his critics have already stated, is not perfect and is not the ultimate, but it is a dramatic step forward from the Bill which I presented and passed through the House of Commons in the late sixties. There are some things about this legislation, as the Minister knows, which concern me. One of the things which concerns me is the blurring of lines between the rules which cover collective bargaining. Yet, necessary standards are needed for more than two-thirds of the workers of this country who have no protection because they are not unionized. Sometimes the lines get blurred and abused. I would have liked to have seen a clause which permitted organized labour and their employers to opt out of the impact of the Labour Code. That may happen the next time this legislation comes before the House, but this is probably my last speech and I will probably not be here. There is no substitute for a negotiated settlement and no substitute for collective agreements.
One of the most significant things which we were able to do in the House of Commons-because we allowed labour to open collective agreements if technology was introduced without sufficient notice-was to force labour and management to include in collective agreements the ways and means to deal with technology. It was brought out in committee that there have not been more than a dozen cases sent to the Canada Labour Relations Board, at the request of unions, which were based on complaints that there was no opportunity to negotiate. Therefore, management has become enlightened. They have become enlightened just in time, because if this country is to continue to produce and generate the capital which is needed for social policy, pensions, maternity leave and so on, we must be a more productive country. We must have a more productive workforce in order to generate the additional capital. We are not only behind Japan, which we hear about all the
Canada Labour Code
time, we are falling very far behind the other countries in the OECD. In Europe, unions have been a way of life, particularly since the second World War. Management in Europe has tended to recognize the social contract. Some of the things which we have attempted to include in this Bill recognize the unique problems of women in the workforce, including sexual harassment. I believe we have at the present moment a very unique worker coming on stream. Unlike 15 years or 30 years ago, the worker today tends to be a knowledgeable worker rather than simply a skilled worker. He or she has had a college or university education. These new workers are mobile. They are intelligent. They face the new world with great confidence and they are not afraid of technology or computerization. They only ask to be informed and consulted and to be listened to. Employers who refuse to recognize that fact do so at their own risk as does the country which does not put through the type of enlightened legislation with the thrust which this Bill has. It is not Utopia but it is a considerable improvement over the basic Labour Code.
What concerns me is that the Department of Labour, the Canada Labour Relations Board and others do not always understand the spirit behind the proposed legislation. What was the intent? Why is the clause written in that way? What did the legislature mean when this clause or that clause was discussed? I would like to give an example which is very close to my heart. In 1966, the most difficult labour situation in Canada was at the waterfront, the longshoring industry. It involved not only Montreal and Vancouver but all of the waterfronts of Canada. Men were treated little better than animals. They had to go every morning to a hiring hall to be selected for employment with no guarantee when they arrived there on a cold day that they would be hired. It was the law of the jungle with strong-arm tactics. There was corruption. It was a very bad situation. Ports like Montreal were strikebound for weeks and weeks. The Smith inquiry was set up to improve the situation. I rejected its report because in my opinion it was based on the premise that the trouble in the ports was essentially caused by employees. I recognized that those employees were stripped of their dignity, and we set out to do something about it. We also recognized, Mr. Speaker, the need for increased productivity. Today the number of employees in the Montreal waterfront is approximately half of what it was in 1968. The productivity is hundreds of per cent greater. Why? Because the worker now goes to work in dignity, in an automobile, with a guaranteed 40 weeks wages out of 52 weeks whether or not there is work. The hiring halls have been eliminated, pension plans have been introduced. Technology is not rejected. It is encouraged because so many cents per tonne coming in through technology, through containerization, find their way into the union for its particular projects, sickness benefits, pensions, or whatever.
This was not accomplished, Mr. Speaker, by myself or the Department. It was accomplished by intelligent use of new legislation. It was accomplished by making it mandatory for all employers to bargain as one and for all unions to bargain as

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
one, thus eliminating the old game of playing one off against the other. If you look at the old Code, I believe Section 132, you will find that we set it up in such a way that these associations would have total jurisdiction over what was called "geographical delineation". I believe that is the way we put it. It simply meant that when negotiating time arrived, management would speak as one voice and so would the union.
In recent years, Mr. Speaker, in the 1980s, the Canada Labour Relations Board seems to me, as an observer, to have lost the sense of what was the intent. So we have a situation now where across the river some intelligent employer is setting up shop with union or non-union people who are prepared to work for less, not bothering to bargain but simply taking advantage of collective agreements which are eventually struck across the river, thereby reintroducing, if you like, the seeds of discontent, the destruction of something which has proven to be successful.
There has not been a major strike in the waterfronts of Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Quebec or Three Rivers in ten years. The workers average between $30,000 and $40,000 a year. They earn it and are entitled to it. Yet the Canada Labour Relations Board, through decisions made in good faith, threatens that situation because it does not understand the spirit behind Section 132. It does not understand the importance of keeping the unions and management together. I mention this as an area which I do hope will be looked at every thoroughly by committee or by the House the next time the Code comes forward for debate. Perhaps Section 132 could be amended to make a little clearer to the members of the Canada Labour Relations Board what was the original intent of that particular section.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I share the views of the officials critic for labour of the Conservative Party. I share his concern for the argument advanced so eloquently by the Adventist Church. However, I must remind him as well that the Rand formula is not exactly breaking new ground. It is something which has been around for decades. It was introduced in the automobile industry. It was meant to provide a solution to people who did not want to belong to a union but who recognized that unions work on their behalf whether or not they are members. I have no opposition to the amendments which provide something whereby people of conscience could remain in the workforce and contribute indirectly to the work of the union.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that this is probably the most important piece of legislation which has gone through the House for some time. It is important because it is, perhaps, a belated recognition by the House and by the Government that unless the climate of co-operation between management and labour is such that the adversarial characteristics will be minimized, and unless the climate in this country is such that management, labour and government can work in unison in co-operation and dignity, we are not going to be able to maintain the flow of private capital to production, because we are still a decade behind the kind of industrial relationships which prevail in many other countries.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments?

Mr. Speaker, in my speech I was highly critical of the lack of participation of Hon. Members of the Liberal Party and of the Conservative Party in committee. I want to correct that. Because of the fact the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) has been here since 1962, and the fact that he has contributed his energy and a big chunk of his life to this House of Commons, one would have expected him to have been the last person to be at the committee meeting at 2 a.m. But he was there at 2 a.m. and then at 9.30 a.m. and throughout the hearings. He was there caring, being constructive and being positive. I thank him for that contribution and I did mean to include him in my comments, along with the Hon. Member for Calgry West (Mr. Hawkes) and the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) who sat there hour upon hour to make this legislation better. I wanted to recognize that and to thank him for his service and the comments he made today.

Mr. Speaker, I assure the hon. gentleman that I did not take any of his remarks the wrong way. I know exactly what he meant and I share his views. I suppose 1 was there, as he was, because I was brought up in a school of thought that you have an obligation to the job you take on, wherever it may be. When work is a pleasure, then you attend to it. When the Minister asked me to join that committee I looked on it as an opportunity in some simple way, through moral persuasion or seduction or even bullying, to come up with a Bill which I felt was non-partisan in nature. At no time in committee did I think we had broken down into pro and anti-labour, pro and anti-Liberal, or pro and anti-anything. I think all of us sensed that our frustration was that if we only had more time, we could do better. I just wanted to say that when you get discouraged, look at the original Bill in 1968 and see what progress we have made in 15 years. It has really been remarkable.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to see that this Bill is finally at third reading stage. As I mentioned when we started the second reading debate on this Bill, our caucus had been working ever since the election in 1980 to have changes made to the Canada Labour Code. I mentioned then that we had asked for a special House order which would allow this legislation to go to committee so that representatives from different groups could appear and we would report back for final disposition in the last couple of days of the sitting. When I hear some of the rhetoric coming from the spokesmen for the Conservative Party, I recognize that it is basically a defensive reaction by a Party which was smoked out a number of times here and in committee. An impartial observer of that committee would tell you that the Conservatives were doing everything they could to stall and not be caught. Their attempts to add more and more witnesses as the week progressed were not to hear more voices but to prevent the Bill from passing.
June 27, 1984
What a bunch of garbage.

1 regret we have had to take this tone in debate but after hearing the wild rhetoric of the official spokesman for the Conservative Party, the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), it is very obvious that they have only looked at this as a political exercise rather than as a very important piece of legislation.
We are getting wild rhetoric from you right now.

Four years ago our caucus toured federal and provincial work sites right across this country. We went to every province and all sorts of industry and came out with a report called Graveyard Shifts: Life and Death on the Job in Canada. We presented that report to successive Ministers of Labour and got up in this House many times asking for changes to the Labour Code. I am glad to see that some of those amendments came forward, even if it took until the fifth year of this Government's rule. It is unfortunate that the actual debate on this legislation did not take place until the last three weeks of this sitting.
I agree with one aspect of what the Conservative representative said, that we should have had more time to study the legislation. I believe there could be amendments made that would strengthen the legislation. There were groups who, had they had more time, could have come forward with suggestions which would have improved the legislation. But that is not the case. We were forced to deal with the Bill within a week in committee. Even though it meant sitting late hours and committee members were fatigued, we agreed to hear from every group who wished to speak. But as our House Leader said the day after this Bill was tabled, we wanted it passed because we recognized that for the most part it was an improvement which would protect the life and safety of more Canadian workers. It would provide legal protection for federal Government employees who come under Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, protection they never had before. We also saw that there were some benefits in maternity leave and child care for those people who come under the Canada Labour Code. I must say that we saw some strictly token efforts in the area of sexual harassment, part-time workers and technological change. But they were improvements and, recognizing this session was coming to an end, we agreed to pass the legislation. We did all in our power to force both the Government to act and the Official Opposition to move on this legislation.
I make no apologies for our position. It was a deliberate attempt by us to get the legislation passed. We recognize that there were some who saw political benefit in not seeing it passed. There are some who felt they could benefit whether or not it passed. But to our way of thinking the women of Canada, the workers of Canada, are much better protected if it is passed, and that was the only goal we had. We accomplished that goal.
Some of the presentations we heard this afternoon at report stage and third reading talked about how the legislation was
Canada Labour Code
improved because the Conservative Party made representations on behalf of the individuals who came forward. However, were the women of Canada who came forward asked by the Conservatives or Liberals if they wanted the maternity leave or child care qualifying period moved up from three months to six months? No, they were not. So when people get up and make sanctimonious speeches about how they represent others, take a look at what they really did.
Which amendments did you present?

Look at the amendments the Conservatives had included in this Bill which will hurt many parents over the next couple of years. I hope we do not have to wait for four years into the next Parliament to make improvements in this legislation. I said earlier that part-time workers were just barely mentioned in this legislation. The technological change provisions are mere tokenism at this stage of the game. There is a lot left to do and I hope that with some improved rules in the House the committee can sit down fairly early in the next Parliament and look at what needs to be done to protect our workers who come under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-34. First of all, I wish to thank Hon. Members for agreeing to deal expeditiously with this Bill. There certainly was a time when we did not think we would be able to have this legislation passed before the House adjourned for the summer. However, I believe that especially the firm resolve of Canadian union organizations, which did not hesitate to make direct representations to the three Parties sitting in the House-as I said, I think this very firm resolve on the part of Canadian unions to see this labour legislation approved, and of course thanks to the efforts of all three political Parties, all this was an incentive for us to take all action necessary to get this Bill through the House, even when it meant sitting very late, on occasion, to expedite consideration of the Bill in committee.
Mr. Speaker, at this point, I would like to pay tribute to all those who helped realize this Bill. I think it is a piece of very important legislation for labour, and I am very proud to say that my senior officials have worked unremittingly for months to prepare these amendments to the Canada Labour Code. They conducted major consultations with all parties concerned in this country. I would like to stress more specifically the support, good advice and enthusiasm of my Deputy Minister, Mr. Mark Daniels, who has helped me enormously during the last few weeks in working towards passage of this Bill.

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
I also wish to mention the very professional and very thorough work done by the two Assistant Deputy Ministers, Mrs. Wendy Porteous and Mr. Bill Kelly, who both took part in consultations on amendments to Part V and Part IV of the Canada Labour Code, and thanks to whom we now have a Bill that, to a considerable extent, meets the aspirations of Canadian unions.
I also wish to offer thanks for the often important but unspectacular work done by many officials in my Department who helped to draft and prepare documents and prepare the Bill, especially Mrs. Elizabeth MacPherson, Mr. Mac Rowe, M. Doug Baldwin, Mr. Jim McLellan, Dr. Ratna Ray, Mrs. Carol Racine and Mr. Peter Sorokan, who all worked to help make this Bill acceptable to both union and management representatives.
Once again, I think it is important to emphasize that we have been able to improve the Canada Labour Code thanks to the many groups in the labour and the business world we were able to consult. Thanks to these consultations which I myself, my predecessors and my officials have had with these representatives during the past years since these consultations took almost two years we were able to define a number of practical and realistic considerations and, especially, to formulate amendments that are progressive and appropriate at this time.
Mr. Speaker, more than ever I am confident that industrial relations in this country will be able to exist in an atmosphere of trust, civility and mutual respect. Undoubtedly, the Bill we are about to adopt today is particularly welcome to the unions, but I think that management representatives who made representations to the Committee understood that it was important to respond to the legitimate claims of the unions. The Bill we are proposing and are about to approve today is a step in the right direction towards improving the job environment and labour relations. I believe that our society, like all other western industrialized societies, will continue to develop rapidly and that this will be due to the incredible rate at which technology is progressing. However, I think that basically, we must have legislation that ensures that all of us, wherever we are, will be treated fairly and equitably. I think that this legislation, which is well-balanced and responds to the legitimate concerns of Canadian workers, nevertheless can be accepted and acknowledge by management as a Bill that is appropriate to our modern society.
I think that one of the major social facts of the eighties is the change in composition of the labour force population. The proportion of women in the labour force has risen over the last thirty years from 22 to 40 per cent, and in 1980, the participation rate of women exceeded 50 per cent. This massive arrival of women on the labour market has obliged people to re-examine their values and governments to rethink their policies.
Twenty years ago, labour policies did not have to consider the family responsibilities of workers. As a general rule, once women were married, they withdrew from the labour force,
while men dedicated themselves to their careers. However, due to a number of reasons that are economic, educational, demographic and psychological in nature, these differences have ceased to exist. Although men no longer dominate the sector of paid employment, women however, still have, though not willingly, a monopoly over unpaid domestic work. That is why they are often unable to take full advantage of their newly won access to paid employment. As many female workers are well aware, interrupting their period of employment to have and raise children reduces their years of seniority and adversely affects their chances of promotion and their eligibility for social benefits.
Mr. Speaker, these are so many irrefutable arguments in favour of the revision of Part III of the Canada Labour Code which I proposed to the House and which will very soon be approved by this Parliament. I have no hesitation in saying that in all my political career, after the cooperative housing program established when I was Minister responsible for urban affairs, this is the second most important social measure which I have had the privilege of being involved with as Minister. I think it is important to point out that the amendments we have submitted to Parliament are definitely to the advantage of Canadian working women, with respect to Labour Code Part III and most of the series of amendments found in Part IV concerning occupational safety and health.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of repeating the details of every aspect of this Bill. They are now well known. During previous interventions in the House, I had the opportunity to elaborate on the major amendments to Parts III, IV and V of the Labour Code.
Since I do not want to speak at length at this stage and would rather conclude my remarks as quickly as possible, I want to say before closing the debate that I was extremely pleased with the reaction of the unions. I want to thank publicly the CLC and the other labour organizations which gave their support to Bill C-34. As Minister of Labour, I was particularly glad to hear so many positive comments about this labour legislation which, I am sure, will stand us in good stead and certainly pave the way for more harmonious labour relations in Canada. I am convinced that the adoption of this Bill will signal the onset of a new era of harmony, understanding and co-operation between the Government of Canada and the Labour movement and, I should hope, between unions and the business community.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge Hon. Members to give unanimous approval to this Bill for which Canadian workers, men and women alike, have waited so long.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We were on questions.

I thank the Member from the Northwest Territories for his intervention. I think I was the Member from Calgary who was referred to.
If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) values the committee process so highly and the commitment that committee members made to that process, how did we end up with only four days in which to hear witnesses and have a clause by clause discussion? How did that happen if it is such a valued process?

Mr. Speaker, I cannot resist the temptation of answering the Hon. Member by saying that, our parliamentary process being what it is and because of recent incidents such as the bell-ringing incident which made us waste valuable time and which was sparked by the Progressive Conservative Party, as were endless, abusive and never-ending debates by the Opposition on many Bills introduced in the House, unfortunately Parliament is forced to sit until the very end of the session and quickly adopt a number of Bills.
Had the Progressive Conservative Party not made us waste so much time in the House, we would probably have had a few extra days to consider Bill C-34 in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the Minister is way off base now and again, and this happens to be a good example.
Canada Labour Code

The Minister will know that the bells rang for democracy and freedom because the Government was attempting to deny adequate examination of legislation. A four-day period to hear witnesses and to deal with legislation clause by clause is another example of the fact that this Government and this Minister in particular-who seems to be a critical Minister with a changed leader and someone of influence-still believe that it is bad for Canadian society to have a process which allows for a little daylight and permits sufficient time to question witnesses and argue for amendments.
Let me ask the Minister the question that I had in mind originally. I was going to compliment him because it is the first time in the life of this Parliament that I had seen a sufficient number of senior officials present at all times during the questioning of witnesses. It is the very first time that any Cabinet Minister of the Government brought senior officials in and left them there to hear witnesses and the questions and arguments. That resulted in 13 amendments, which is considerably more than the average, even though the time frame was short. Does the credit belong to the Deputy Minister or was it the Minister's idea that those senior officials be present?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the example Parliament has given us with Bill C-34 should normally be followed for all pieces of legislation. Although the Progressive Conservative Members claim that they have not had enough time to consider this Bill, I believe that they have had ample time to consider the principle of the Bill at second reading stage, to receive all the submissions they wanted in the Committee, to examine these submissions and even to question certain witnesses, to examine the Bill clause by clause with the Minister and the departmental officials, and finally to come back to this House after working hard in the Committee to give passage to Bill C-34 in one day.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, we should spend as much time as we have spent on Bill C-34 at all stages for a great many other pieces of legislation. I believe that this Bill received the attention it deserved. With a lot of good will on both sides, we showed that we could study a very important Bill within a few days, as is regularly the case in the British Parliament, where even the most important and controversial Bills are passed within a few days. Which brings me to say that, in the next Parliament, I hope that we shall have the cooperation of the Progressive Conservatives, who will still be in the Opposition, to amend parliamentary procedure so that we may deal with our legislative program within a reasonable time-
In the interests of the Canadian public!

-and especially, as my friend has suggested, in the interests of the Canadian public.

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any other questions? Debate. The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes).

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with somewhat mixed emotions. I would like to assure the Minister that as the next Government we would welcome his input in the future. We fully intend to be that Government and we fully intend to demonstrate a little bit of openness and give sufficient time to hear witnesses and as well ensure sufficient process to allow Members of Parliament to make a real contribution to legislation which will pay off in better government for Canadians.
Let me begin by complimenting the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) who spoke at some length today. He did an excellent job of encapsulating the process, the type of amendments we were able to include in this legislation, the reasons behind them, and the difficulties that we as a Party had to overcome to achieve those gains.
Having said that, let me revert to what I said at the beginning, that I had somewhat mixed emotions. This process has brought back some memories to me. One was my maiden speech in this House in 1979 when I tried to explain that the exploration of the oil and gas industry was really an occupation fraught with danger. I did not think Members of this Chamber really understood that industry or the difficulties it faces. I stand here today knowing the National Energy Program is in place and some of the consequences from it are a pretty clear indication that I did not do my job in 1979. Obviously I was not persuasive enough in this Chamber.
I also remember July, 1950, some 34 years ago. That is a long time in the lives of any of us. The last two or three weeks have reminded me of a switchman on the Canadian National Railways. In the middle of the night he was swept off the top of a box car by wires belonging to the Alberta Government Telephones and fell on an embankment. Workers of the City of Calgary were digging a ditch alongside the railroad. He rolled down the embankment and under the wheels of a Canadian National train and was killed. That was July, 1950, 34 years ago. The mixed emotions come because that man was my father. I was 16 at the time. I have since participated in a process where something like that is a little less likely to happen today, and of that I am proud.
Hear, hear!

But mixed with that sense of pride is anger. I am angry at a process that trades workers' safety for some of the other garbage that was brought forward in the Bill. We have to accept some of the garbage in the process. The protection for the Canadian people that has been worked out in the British Parliament and in this Parliament is the time to examine, the time to hear witnesses, and the time to make sure that we are not making a mistake. It is a terrible choice to have to pick between a worker's safety and the abrogation of
the process. It is not right. It was not right in the beginning and it is not right here today.
A few minutes ago the Minister talked about parliamentary reform. I would love to see a reform that did not allow for this kind of abrogation process. I would like to see a reform that required a responsible Minister to sit through every hour of public hearings on a piece of legislation which the Minister proposed. I would like to see Ministers sit and listen to witnesses before Ministers make up their minds and nod their heads yes or no as to whether an amendment is acceptable. I do not think that second-hand information is sufficient.
I saw the Constitution of Canada, the fundamental law of this land, amended. I knew that many of the groups who put their hearts and souls into their submissions came to this city and appeared before the Committee on the Constitution in the belief that they could be and would be heard. Many Members heard them. But the decision-makers all too frequently did not. That is why I asked the Minister whose idea it was to have senior officials before our committee. In four and a half years that is the first time I have seen so many officials in Committee, and I compliment them for their capacity to listen and, ultimately, to have some influence on the Minister. One thing I have learned is that the Opposition very, very rarely has any influence on a Minister. All a Member of the Opposition can do is to try to persuade some other people who in turn might have some influence on the Minister. In this case that is influence through the bureaucratic mechanism.
There is a better way, and that is to force the Minister to be part of the process, to listen to witnesses, and to give individuals the opportunity to persuade a Minister directly.
I mentioned earlier today that I was somewhat angry at the Canadian Labour Congress. In standing here today I do not know whether to blame the people representing the Canadian Labour Congress. I know what they did, but I cannot be privy as to why they did it. People from the Canadian Labour Congress came before our committee and said: "Hold your nose and pass the Bill." We asked them how we could make the Bill a little bit better. We asked them what was right and what was wrong with the Bill. They said: "Hold your nose and pass the Bill". I think that is short-changing the one to two million members of the Congress, Mr. Speaker. I think the leadership of the Canadian Labour Congress knowingly or unknowingly short-changed its membership.
We do not get many opportunities in this Chamber to change the Canada Labour Code. The Leader of the Progre-sive Conservative Party said: "We like the thrust of these amendments. Yes, we will do our bit to make sure they get through before the end of this Parliament." In that atmosphere, perhaps the Canadian Labour Congress did not trust the NDP or the Liberals, but I think the Canadian Labour Congress had an obligation to share with committee members its thoughts on how to make Bill C-34 better. If this Bill is inadequate and if there are clauses that could have been included and they were not, the Canadian Labour Congress deserves some of the blame. That has worried me. In committee I have pointed it out to the Congress. But if the Congress is
June 27, 1984

indistinguishable from a political Party, then an atmosphere of suspicion is created which makes it more difficult to function together on behalf of the workers and on behalf of Canadian society. What part of the remarks made in this Chamber today or in committee will the Canadian Labour Congress and its affiliates choose to reprint in its newsletters sent out to the membership? Will there be a fair and accurate reflection of the debate and the reality of the process? There will probably not be because the Canadian Labour Congress has attached itself to a political Party in this Chamber.
When this process began, I was almost totally convinced that the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party had no interest in passing the Bill. I stand here today with the suspicion that that was really true some three weeks ago. The only reason the Bill was brought forward was to create an issue for a political campaign.
The filibustering of the New Democratic Party on other pieces of legislation jammed our calendar and kept us here one day until five o'clock in the morning. That provides evidence consistent with that belief. It was trying to create a climate in which to go into a federal general election, having missed the opportunity to provide a better health and safety climate rather than accomplishing it. That would have been the strongest electoral position for the New Democratic Party. Also it would have been a strong electoral position for the Liberal Party of Canada.
That was our concern right from the start. If that was its strategy, it got a hell of a surprise. No Party worked harder than our Party at making sure that the Bill was examined as well as it could be within the time frame allowed and that it was returned to the Chamber in an acceptable fashion or the best we could make it.
The tragedy is that the process could have been better. The Bill could have been better. We would have welcomed an opportunity to help. The Government let us down. For that, we should all be a little sad and not get carried away with joy. It is better to have tried as hard as we could than to have settled for second best, for a process which did not allow us to try.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? On debate, the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen).

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be very brief. I understand that we are working under a schedule, but I have a few comments to make. I am, without any equivocation, very happy at the results we are seeking today. No one with experience in collective bargaining or the process in which we are engaged here-and there are some similarities in these processes-expects a perfect package. That is not what this process is all about. The idea is to make progress, hopefully substantial progress. By whatever variety of methods we have used to arrive at this point today, the Labour Code Bill before us is substantial progress for the working people of Canada.
Canada Labour Code
I congratulate all of those people who have been involved. I will not rise to the bait of my Conservative colleague who spoke a few minutes ago by responding to what he said. That is not the mood I want to create at this point.
Congratulate the Minister.

I will congratulate the Minister of Labour and his two predecessors. I congratulate the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan), the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet).
I congratulate the Canadian Labour Congress and the representatives of hundreds of democratic organizations of working people across the country who had, directly or indirectly, some input into this Bill. All their advice was not accepted, but that is not the way we work. That is not the way the labour movement works. That is not the way industrial relations works.
I am sad at the delay in the introduction of the Bill. We could have had more time to deal with it in committee and in the House. However, I do not know whether we would have achieved any more substantial progress than is to be found in the measures now included in Bill C-34. Time was provided for extensive consultations between the various Parties. Not only were the unions, the Government and other political Parties involved, but many employer groups were consulted over the last three or four years as well. It did not all happen in one, two or three days in committee. My colleagues in all Parties in the House know that, despite their protestations to the contrary. It has been a very worth-while exercise.
In relation to the process of collective bargaining, this process here today reminds me that the best contract agreements are achieved in the minutes preceding a strike deadline. Of course the House of Commons does not face a strike deadline, but it faces an election in the very near future. Strikes and elections have something in common. We see the end of a particular opportunity and no one wants to gamble on the outcome. When there is a chance of achieving significant progress, the question with which we are all faced is whether or not we want to gamble on blowing the whole thing. This is what any union has to face in a strike deadline situation. It has to decide whether it will settle for what is on the table or squeeze out a little more in the last few minutes.
My colleagues and I faced up to that option. We decided that it was not worth the risk. When it comes to an election, we are all in the lap of the gods that are known as the voters. They are unpredictable, just as it is unpredictable when a union or a company has to decide to strike or lock people out rather than settle for a compromise.
My purpose in being here is to obtain the best results, at the least cost, for the people I represent. That is the same job I had when I represented a union and it is the same job I have today in representing some 75,000 constituents in the riding of Kootenay West. My riding has a very large body of industrial workers as well as government employees, more provincial than federal. It has many working people as well as a mixed population of various different economic interests.

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
If this matter poses a choice of either swallowing my pride or trying to play hero-whether it be a working class hero, a political hero or anything else-if I have to trade that off to obtain benefits for the people I am sworn to represent, I will choose to get results every time because my people are a lot more important than I am and that is my job.
I should like to refer to one problem in industrial relations. It is probably one of the most misunderstood human activities in the world. It is misunderstood by many trade unionists, managers and employers alike, and it is vastly misunderstood by the public at large. This is also reflected in the misunderstanding which is often evident in the halls of government. At one time I was a representative, both full-time and part-time, of the International Woodworkers of America. I was also president of the Nelson, Trail and District Labour Council for some three terms. Very often I took the opportunity to visit the high schools in my constituency and talk with students. Very few students, even in areas which were involved in mining and lumber, ever thought that after graduation they would have to work for wages for a living. This is one of the problems with television and the other media in this age of ours. Everyone thinks they will be professionals, semi-professionals or independent business people. I just ain't so. People also have misconceptions because they do not understand what their role in life will likely be and they thus do not feel the need to understand what industrial relations and unions are all about. Unions, industrial relations and personnel management are not people who spend 90 per cent of their time negotiating. Anyone in industrial relations spends 90 per cent of his or her working time on the grievance procedure, which is, in turn, the single most misunderstood instrument by managers and even active unionists. It is not essentially a method for finding fault. It is simply an attempt at an orderly mechanism to resolve possible errors in judgment. That is all it is. We require similar appeal methods both in the courts and in industrial relations.
What makes me happy about this Bill is that it begins-and it is not the first beginning as we have made attempts before- to recognize some of these realities. The process that we used has recognized some of the realities that exist in the industrialized world. It is not about perfection. We are not dealing with fairy tales. We are dealing with the lives of people. There are gains that have been made in terms of maternity leave. For women, we have made some but not great progress in recognizing the need for protection against sexual harassment in the workplace. As well, there are a great many measures that tend to build a more intelligent system for enforcing occupational health and safety in the workplace. I just mention that one area. There is substantial progress in that area in the Bill.
1 would like to pay particular tribute to my fellow Members of the NDP Task Force on Occupational Health and Safety, the Hon. Member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), and the Hon. Member for Kootenay-East Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) who, along with myself, spent three years going back and forth across the country, trying to get the maximum input into what we then
thought would be an early consideration of this subject in the House of Commons.
We do not feel that time was wasted, because we learned something. Even those of us who had some past experience in this area learned a great deal. We were able to communicate some of what we had learned to those in management and in the labour movement as well as to those in Government. As well, we recognized the fact that the Government was carrying on consultations with other people, mostly through its departmental officials, but some very personally, with a direct concern outside of the political sphere.
One thing that does concern me tonight is the final statement of the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). I do not know whether it was a promise or a threat. I will paraphrase what he said. His final phrase went something like this: "We look forward to looking at the legislation again in detail in the fall". I cannot foretell what the electorate will do in the forthcoming election, but I do know what a certain provincial government in British Columbia has done in the last few months by looking in detail at previous good, progressive labour legislation which used to exist on the statute books of that province. They are attempting to turn it upside down.
My concept of freedom and socialism has always been that it is "a responsible society governed by responsible men and women in a responsible manner." I have always rejected paternalism and I do not like paternalism today. That has caused me to disagree from time to time with some other people who call themselves socialists as well as many people of other political persuasions. I do not like a government that tries to do things for people. I prefer to have a government that accords to democratic institutions and communities in society the power to help themselves.
The Code before us helps to redistribute some of that power, and devolve some of that power and responsibility into the workplace, to the workers, managers, and employers, and set up a framework in which they can co-operate and work together, to try to produce the greatest good for the greatest number. That is what it is all about. That is why we should be here. I support the Bill. I thank everybody involved. I congratulate them once more for having participated in what was a healthy exercise and what will be, I hope, something that produces good results for the working people of Canada and all other Canadians.
Are there any questions or comments?
