Mr. Speaker, to be very brief and at the request of my colleague for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), and my colleague for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne), who was most happy to hear my speech this afternoon, I would like to add a few words and say that, as far as we are concerned we have been very happy to receive the suggestions made both by labour and by management concerning Bill C-34. In this regard, I believe that there have been important discussions in recent months, not to say in recent years, about possible changes to the Canada Labour Code. When the representatives appeared before us, they indicated that they were in favour of the Bill generally, and as I said at the report stage, what we were asked by employer groups was to try to have a balanced Bill as they were themselves aware of the need for changes. I see the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) who agrees with me that this Bill is very important for the workers. He even told us that he was president of a union. He therefore speaks for the workers and probably because of that he was in touch with his colleague for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) and he asked him to support the Bill and to move amendments so that the Bill could be passed.
Mr. Speaker, a number of changes have been made, especially in Clause 28 and Clause 29, and 1 am referring to the matter of notice of technological change. I remember that both labour and management agreed on this point. More specifically, I recall that the Association of Canadian Bankers agreed with the 120-day notice so that workers could see what could be done in terms of these new developments.
Another important point, as the Minister of Labour pointed out, is that today, women represent nearly 50 per cent of the labour force, and that it was high time to amend the Canada Labour Code so as to take into consideration this category that is now on the labour market. That is why, when considering Clause 6 and Clause 59.2, we had to give a number of rights to workers that were both necessary and timely. In the Canada Labour Code, as the legislation stands now, employees with twelve months service have certain rights and are eligible for a certain number of weeks of leave, and now, the Government has introduced an amendment to reduce this period to six months.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage, however, since we want to adopt this Bill, I wish to thank my colleagues on both sides of the House who took part in the debate, listened to witnesses, took part in the debate on second reading, and after the second reading stage, heard many witnesses in rather quick and repetitive succession-in other words, we had a pretty busy agenda, and at the clause-by-clause stage, we finished at one o'clock in the morning last Thursday-I wish to thank both Opposition parties for their co-operation in helping us pass amendments. We on this side of the House accepted the amendments proposed by the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party also made its point.
Canada Labour Code
My hon. friend from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Male-part) who is a former member of the FTQ-
Still a member!

speechtext: Are there any further questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I want to put my comments on the Bill before us in the context of my final speech in the House of Commons. I ask for your latitude, Sir, and the indulgence of the House for a few moments to allow me to express some thoughts that I feel deeply as I take leave of this great institution after 12 years.
I found it instructive to re-read the first speech I made here. I criticized then high government spending, called for a better deal for western Canada and urged greater Canadian attention to the global problems of security and development. Today in my final speech, I could repeat these themes with even greater urgency. Plus (a change, plus c'est la me me chose.
These 12 years have been the most informative, educational and challenging years of my life. For the rest of my life I will be grateful for the opportunity, and indeed the honour, of walking onto the floor of the House of Commons to represent my constituents. It is they who sent me here and it is they whom I must thank first. The people, first of Edmonton Strathcona and then of Edmonton South, placed their confidence in me during four elections. I have tried to help them as best I could.

June 27, 1984
Canada Labour Code
Of course, my political supporters and election campaigners were instrumental in bringing me forward. No politician ever had a stronger team. They stayed with me even when they did not always agree with me. My staff, both in Ottawa and in Edmonton, provided me with loyal assistance and hard work through the years. As well, I owe a debt of thanks to the officials in the House, the Parliamentary Library and Research Bureau, as well as to the messengers, pages and guards who ease the path of Members.
I take away with me friendships with Members on all sides of the House, friendships that I will always treasure. I have benefited especially from the counsel of members of my own Party and I thank my colleagues for their consideration of me and of the views I have expressed over the years. It has been a privilege to serve under three distinguished Leaders of our Party, the Hon. Robert Stanfield, the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) who will become the next elected Prime Minister of Canada. As for my family, I cannot adequately express my appreciation for their devotion to me.
There is no practical way to sum up in a few minutes one's experiences with so many events in the past 12 years. However, there is one dominant thought that I want to share with my colleagues as I prepare to depart, and that is, the desire that I and so many people have today for collective security and economic and social justice in the world.
Science and technology have made today's world a dazzling place and offer the potential for every human being to enjoy a life of quantity and quality. But just as our age abounds with the promise of life, it is fraught with the threat of death. While science can transform the world into a more habitable and safer place for everyone, it has also unleashed the potential for global destruction.
The massive buildup of nuclear arsenals and conventional weapons could wipe out most of the earth's species including mankind in a matter of hours. Conflicts rage in all parts of the globe. Chaotic imbalances of food and population hold a quarter of the world hostage to hunger, disease and despair. The earth's population is burgeoning and its already strained resources recklessly squandered while the environment is precariously poised on the edge of disaster. Human rights are repressed on a massive scale; millions are forced to flee their homes. Can anyone doubt that our world today is in crisis?
Two issues above all others stand out in the struggle for peace in the world today: disarmament and development. The reduction of nuclear arms is at the centre of East-West relations. Accelerated economic development is the theme of North-South relations. There is not a human being today unaffected by the vast ramifications of these two global issues. Untold millions are directly caught up in the expanding militarism and deprivation of our time; intensified military competition in turn worsens economic pressures on both developed and developing countries. The deterioration in the world economy has exacerbated political instability and social crises in Third World countries which have a potential for setting off widening conflicts. How the two issues are resolved
will determine the prospects for true human security around the world.
We must seriously ask ourselves how much time is spent in Parliament on finding equitable solutions to these two paramount issues. Are we not so caught up with the daily pressures of parliament that we have no time for the wider view? This problem of priorities has troubled me for some time. I remind Hon. Members that stopping the arms race is not just a spiritual desire but is essential for world survival. Closing the rich-poor gap is no longer just a matter of striving for social justice but is essential to the continued development of the industrialized North. Some form of world law is necessary to resolve major international conflicts without violence and to retain the human and material resources needed to redress the global problems which confront us. Management of the planet by nations agreeing to co-operate in their common interest, thus ensuring that the promise of life prevails over the now suffocating threat of death, must be achieved.
All of this, Sir, is the work of the United Nations, the only global instrument we have to protect the global community. But today, critics maintain that the United Nations has not fulfilled its promise. The failure, however, lies not in the UN but in those nations that bypass the UN except when it suits their narrowly defined purposes. The Secretary General of the UN, Perez de Cuellar, has said that "the world is perilously near a new international anarchy," and has called for a recommitment by nations to the Charter as the UN prepares to observe its 40th anniversary in 1985.
What can-what must-Canada do now to strengthen the international machinery of the UN system? Drawing on our influence with Commonwealth countries, our increasing contacts with the Francophone countries of Africa and our evolving links with Asian and Latin American countries, Canada could stimulate the development of new coalitions of interest. The rigidities of bloc voting that have stultified the UN in recent years must give way to more universal expressions of concern and action on such pressing questions as peacekeeping, economic development assistance, global economic negotiations, human rights and environmental problems. Canada's success in developing consensus positions at the Law of the Sea Conference could be repeated in other areas. The UN is waiting for such a country to fill a leadership void in the crucial issues of disarmament and development, the two key issues which are at the root of the struggle for peace.
By putting a new focus on human rights, Canada could contribute to significant progress in these two fields. Human rights today are no longer confined to civil and political liberties, though much work remains to be done to guarantee rights in those areas. Human rights must also be protected in economic and social areas of life, and the UN has concentrated much of its activity here. Increasingly, human rights are associated with the right to physical security, and in an age of unending nuclear arms proliferation with a massive destructive capacity, the human rights of every person in the world are jeopardized today.
June 27, 1984

Canada, the country which pioneered the dispatching of peacekeeping forces to trouble spots, could now strengthen the machinery of peace by working to obtain an international inspection organization able to monitor disarmament using both satellites and on-sight inspection, by verifying arms agreements and by observing world military deployments. A true security system needs such an organization able to act with some authority.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in the field of development, Canada, working with like-minded countries, could stimulate greater concern about the straggering effects on the developing countries of the rising debt burden, monetary policies of the industrialized countries and trade barriers. The failure of the North to recognize that its own economic recovery depends on the ability of the growing markets of the South to buy has crippled global economic development. Millions face starvation with little hope for improvement. The pledge of Canada in the Throne Speech of December 7, 1983, to reach .5 per cent of GNP in official development assistance in 1985 and to reach .7 per cent in 1990 is an indication of human concern. However, the lesson of the 1970s was that development aid is but a fraction of what needs to be done to build the economies of the South.
The independent North-South Institute has laid down a program of action. Canada, through the UN, should work to expand the resources and quotas of the International Monetary Fund so that it provides greater help to the least developed. It should take an active part in efforts to initiate a process of basic reform of world trade and financial arrangements; contribute actively to negotiations within the GATT and preparatory discussions regarding a new trade round; play a leadership role in efforts to further integrate the developing countries into the GATT system; act against protectionist trade barriers; develop a new strategy of international development co-operation in harmony with the UN's international development strategy for the 1980s, and promote greater public understanding of the development process. The last point-public awareness-was considered so important by the parliamentary task force on North-South relations that its first recommendation called upon the Government to devote 1 per cent of official development assistance to encourage the awareness and involvement of Canadians in global concerns. Nongovernmental organizations working in the development and disarmament areas have become part of the landscape. Because they involve so many Canadians at the local level, they are capable, with more government support, of building a climate of public opinion which can be an enormous strength for a government to move ahead on UN strategies.
Canada with its history and geography, its freedom and democracy, its resources and technology, and its space and industry, is ideally placed to work for the conditions of peace. As I take my leave of this great institution, that is my wish and my prayer for us all. Au revoir and good luck to us all.

speechtext:
The question is on the following motion: Mr. Ouellet, seconded by Mrs. Hervieux-Payette, moved that Bill C-34, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code and the Financial Administration Act, be now read the third time and do pass.
Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt this motion?

Agreed.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the third time and passed.
The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-33, an Act to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Transport) moved:
speechtext:
That Bill C-33, be amended by adding immediately after line 5 at page 15 the following:
"21. Notwithstanding anything in the Western Grain Stabilization Act, where, prior to the end of the year ending July 31, 1984, the Minister determines that stabilization payments will be made in respect of the year, interim stabilization payments to participants in respect of the year shall, on the requisition of the Minister, be paid out of the Stabilization Account, whether or not the year has ended, on account of the stabilization payments that will be made in respect of the year to participants, based on such information required to be considered at the end of the year in determining stabilization payments as is available to the Minister at the time he first determines that stabilization payments will be made in respect of the year." and by renumbering the subsequent clause accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, after a very long and interesting debate which dealt with matters of labour, I am pleased to be able to introduce measures which will have an important impact upon the lives of so many western Canadian grain farmers. I do not believe it will require a lot of explanation for Members in the Chamber as to the objectives and purposes of this Bill. It is a matter which has been widely discussed and entertained in various Question Periods, committee hearings and debates. However, I think it is important to underline the fact that the amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act will serve to improve what is already a very important and substantial piece of legislation for the protection and income security of western farmers. We will present amendments which will add to the protection and income security substantially by offering an alternative mechanism for the payment of pay-outs by which the Western Grain Stabilization Program can support the income position of the farmers.

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
We all recognize that in the last two or three years western farmers have been squeezed between cash receipts and the expenses with which they are faced. With the depression which is apparent in some areas of the pricing of grains on the international market, it is very important that the Western Grain Stabilization Act be flexible and adaptable to respond to those conditions. One of the flaws which was recognized was that the formulas were not able to incorporate the additional sales and volume which occurred at the same time as expenses rose. Therefore, the fund was not able to respond effectively to the income requirements over the past two or three years. It is quite clear that amendments had to be made in order to ensure that the calculations arrived at would reflect the realities of both the international price situation and, at the same time, reflect the cost problems which western farmers face.
I would suggest to the House that the new pay-out mechanism is not a replacement of the existing legislation but is a secondary pay-out mechanism which will make the program more sensitive to cost and price variations. The present trigger mechanism, which is based upon the net cash flow over a five-year period, will be a continuing part of the Bill. But, the secondary pay-out mechanism, which relates more to the unit cost, will also be available. Therefore, we will be able to trigger pay-outs which will incorporate additional volume or inflationary tendencies.
I realize that there have been a number of recommendations, proposals and alternatives brought forward over a period of time, but in our judgment this will be the most effective way of ensuring that the Western Grain Stabilization Program is one which can be sensitive and flexible to the current needs of western farmers.
It is also important to note the significance of changing the time period in which calculations will be made from the calendar year to the crop year to ensure that there can be a more immediate pay-out. Rather than having to wait for nine or ten months until the end of the calendar year, calculations will now be made at the end of the crop year-on July 31. Therefore, we will be in a position to make the pay-out in the early fall, in October or November.
The amendment which relates to the participation of eligible spouses simply removes a discriminatory feature of the previous legislation. I think all Members of the House will welcome that amendment.
Finally, the major amendment allows participants to withdraw from the program once every ten years. That amendment protects both the stability of the fund and allows a certain amount of choice which can be exercised by the participants if they feel at some point in time that they no longer require protection.
Over all, the amendments are in the best interests of the western farmers. They will help farmers who are presently experiencing cash shortages. We hope this situation will not continue. We hope that through these amendments the stabilization fund can meet its basic requirements and obligations.
The amendment which we have just introduced at report stage is exceptional in that it introduces an interim payment for this year only. This will allow us to make a special response to the plight of the western Canadian farmers at this time. The interim payment, we feel, can be justified because there have been no pay-outs for the last several years.
I know Hon. Members have recommended during committee hearings a continual interim payment provision. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that while it sounds all right in theory, in practice it would be an impractical provision simply because of the inability to calculate the kind of pay-outs for which farmers might be eligible. It is subject to a number of factors which cannot be predicted with any high level of accuracy such as international prices, volumes, costs, all of which can vary from month to month. For us to be continually under the obligation or requirement to make interim payments would mean we would always be making payments without having an accurate prognosis of what the total payment would be after the crop year had closed. Therefore, I believe, Mr. Speaker, we can justify the interim payment amendment, but if we got into an annual interim payment, we would constantly be in a high level of uncertainty as to what those payments would be. It could happen, if you would allow the scenario, Mr. Speaker, at some point in time, under some pressure from Hon. Members opposite, the Conservative Party in particular and perhaps the NDP, which will be opposite for years to come, that we might make an interim payment and then find out, after the calculations were made, that the payment was too large and that the farmers would have to return the money or we would have to pass special legislation.
I would suggest that while in principle it sounds like a good idea, the practicality of it would not be particularly useful. Therefore, I would recommend to Hon. Members of the House that they accept our judgment that while an interim payment can be warranted this year, generally it would be prudent simply to allow the payments to occur after the crop year has closed. As I said earlier, the amendments which we have introduced as part of the Bill will allow those payments to be made in a reasonably short period of time after the close of the crop year.
The purpose of these amendments is to ensure that the Western Grain Stabilization Fund is one which is appropriate to the circumstances and will be most helpful for western Canadian farmers in this period of real need. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that it does underline the ongoing and continuing commitment of this Government to improve the position of western farmers, to provide for a number of initiatives which demonstrate that we want to provide for a good and secure agricultural system in western Canada because we all recognize that it is certainly a major backbone not only of the western Canadian economy but of the entire Canadian economy. Through good legislation and good initiatives, we are able to provide those two things.
I know from some comments of Hon. Members on second reading, that they tend to overlook some of the accomplish-
June 27, 1984

ments which have been achieved by this House and by the Government over the past couple of years. I only point to the major payment of $651 million for the Crow benefit which is being provided-
It is all going to the railways. How does that benefit the farmers?

We have put in place a superb new system of arriving at decision-making in western Canada through the mechanism of the Western Grain Transportation Act. We have just put in $150 million to double the order of hopper cars. We have a new plan for branchline rehabilitation. There is a new $520 million program which will virtually complete the entire network of branchlines, which is something which western farmers have been anxious about. As well we have provided for a reserve fund to allow for new innovative measures and to respond-as I pointed out to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) from time to time-to certain initiatives in the area of the Stettler subdivision and other important areas. I want to point to the measures which were introduced in the last Budget allowing the one time RRSP investment by farmers who are retiring in order to alleviate the problems of capital gains. These amendments we are bringing forward today is simply one step in a series of initiatives which this Government has taken in order to make sure western Canadian farmers are well served and that the western Canadian farm economy will be a prosperous one.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this evening to take part in this debate and, in particular, to respond to the Minister. First of all, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that what we are about to pass this evening is an improvement over what we have had. I do not believe there is really much question about that. We certainly want to give the Government credit for doing this, but let me stop right there as far as handing out accolades is concerned, because I feel that that is as far as it goes. We on this side have been urging the Government to bring forward amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act for about a year and a half. We believe there are other ways we could have amended the Bill which would have made it more flexible. The Minister talks about flexible and adaptable amendments. We did not have enough time in committee. The Government mentioned this measure in its Throne Speech on December 7. Yet we did not receive it in committee until almost the end of May. We got it through committee as quickly as we could to make sure the Government could not blame us in the Opposition for not passing the Bill. If we had had it in committee in January or February, we certainly could have looked at other amendments. In fact, we did not even get a chance to look at the amendment of the Government until just now because the amendments we moved were ruled out of order at committee and we were told that the government amendment would also be out of order because of the royal prerogative. Therefore, in essence, we are looking at the government amendment for the first time right now.
Western Grain Stabili2ation Act
I would like to submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government had truly been serious about looking at the problems in the Western Grain Stabilization Act, it would have acted a lot more responsibly by ensuring that we had a chance to look at it in committee.
There are many ways to adjust the formula-to use the words of the Minister-to make it flexible and adaptable enough to meet the purpose of the Bill. The purpose of the Bill is to stabilize incomes of the western grain farmers by protecting them against sharp declines in the net cash flow. Statistically, we could have looked at a three-year moving average. There were all kinds of things we could have done in terms of studies which would not have affected the actuarial soundness of the Bill. There are all kinds of ways we could have considered to amend the Bill without jeopardizing the financial stability of the Bill. Yet, because of the way the Government managed its affairs, we did not have a chance to do that. I find that rather sad because we do have a very good Committee on Agriculture. As a rule we act in quite non-partisan ways and are generally interested in seeing that things happen in the best interests of Canadian agriculture. Yet we were not given an opportunity to do that. I feel that that is sad. We all suffer, ourselves, the Government and, above all, the people who have sent us here to serve them, because I do not think they are going to get the kinds of amendments they could have had if we had had more time in committee.
There are four amendments in the Bill to which the Minister referred. A very complicated triggering mechanism is going to be used. I could read it to the Minister and I am sure that if we had a chance to question him, he could not explain it to us because it is so complex. However, it will be a mechanism which is more responsive and will trigger some pay-outs in this crop year of something like $300 million and in the next crop year of something like $400 million. While we agree that the amendments which are there are going to be helpful in the immediate term as far as putting cash into the producers' pockets is concerned, I am not so sure it is the right triggering mechanism. I am sure we could have come up with a better one had we had more chance at committee. The Minister said that "our" judgment-obviously, he means that of the Government, the Treasury benches-is that this is the most effective amendment. How does he know that? Surely the committee could have determined which would have been the most effective amendments to put forward. At least we would have had a better opportunity to look at some of the other proposals which came forward.
The problem is being changed to a crop year basis which is, to my mind, a mixed blessing. If you are to have an effective stabilization program the pay-out should be made as quickly as possible after a crop loss. In this country we operate around the growing season. If you harvest a poor crop in the fall of
1984,	you will need some help to get your crop in the ground next year. Ideally you should have some money in your hands from this program when you put in your crop in the spring of
1985.	Yet moving to a crop year eliminates that possibility.

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
It is fine to say that this will make the program more responsive, but if the Minister understood anything about farming he would not be saying the things he did about this amendment. If that is the extent of the Minister's knowledge of western agriculture, then I fear for his new leader, particularly if this Minister is his chief lieutenant in western Canada. He has demonstrated tonight that he knows very little about western agriculture.
The Minister went on to talk about how in theory an interim payment sounds fine but in actual practice it does not work. To be polite, that is a bunch of nonsense. The Government has made two interim payments under the present legislation, and the amendment we moved in committee simply suggested that the Minister may authorize an interim payment. It did not compel the Government to do so. The Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) made a very good point in committee when he said we do not want to tie the hands of future governments. This amendment will only allow an interim payment for the present crop year.
What is wrong with an amendment which states that the Minister may authorize an interim payment? He does not have to do it on a regular basis but the authorization is there if it looks like there is going to be a substantial payment and an interim payment would benefit the producer. Surely that should be the result of properly designed legislation. Then we would not get into this nonsensical scenario where every time we require a pay-out we have to go through this procedure so the producers will have some money in their hands.
This amendment should have been in the House probably three or four months ago. Then producers could have had the benefit of the money in the fund. By the way, there was $864 million in this fund at the end of December, 1983. We did not hold it up. Even the NDP was with us on this one, thank goodness. They get their heads out of the sand once in a while and see the things that should be done for farmers. Everyone on this side was in favour and it should have been done a lot sooner.
Also, I urge the Government, when it makes an interim payment, to make it as large as it can. Members opposite have talked about a 50 per cent or 60 per cent interim payment, but I see nothing wrong with an interim payment of 75 per cent or 80 per cent. That is the basis on which the Canadian Wheat Board establishes initial prices.
In addition, the Government talks about agricultural initiatives. This Government has done absolutely nothing for agriculture in this session. There was one minor Bill which doubled the cash advances on western grain, and dealt with increases in farm credit rates. A motion from this side by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) to reduce the tax on-farm-fuels went to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for study. A motion by the Hon. Member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) concerning the concept of agribonds went to that same committee. When this Government talks about what it has done for Canadian agriculture, I am sure farmers all across the country know what a hollow ring that has to it.
We are pleased to do what we can to get this Bill through this evening so that western farmers at least have the benefit of a big pile of cash the Government has been sitting on for far too long.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the report stage of a Bill which amends the Western Grain Stabilization Act to provide a pay-out of some $250 million to $300 million to western farmers as soon as possible. The Minister mentioned that the Government decided to opt for a one-time interim payment provision. The Bill also contains changes in the formula from five years to three years, and adds to what is already a fairly complex formula something that will be known as "the per unit net cash outflow" component. There has also been a change in the treatment of spouses. Where both husband and wife are involved in the farming operation, both will be permitted to participate in grain levies and any pay-outs that might accrue. There is a new provision which will permit participants in the program to withdraw every ten years. Because the Bill came into effect in 1976, this means that in 1986, 1996 and every ten years thereafter the producer can opt out of the program.
In 1976 our Party raised the issue of some basic shortcomings in this program. We reiterated some of them in committee. I think it is fairly well understood by farmers that it is a very inadequate means of guaranteeing farmers' income, but that was never the intention of the Bill in the first place. It had very little to do with that, but everything to do with guaranteeing incomes to the Prairie region of Canada.
In its application the Bill has some very real inequities. It is available to people who want to opt into the program, and approximately 70 per cent or 75 per cent of farmers have decided to participate. I submit the inequity occurs when wheat and barley growers in parts of Canada other than the Wheat Board region find themselves covered by the general Agricultural Stabilization Act and have indeed received payments under that Act which were not available to farmers in the Wheat Board region who decided not to participate in the Western Grain Stabilization Act. There is some built-in discrimination which creates a wall around a certain region or a province. Because producers decide to opt out of a program, they are forever after ineligible as well for the programs financed nationally.
There is also a real inequity in the financing of the two programs. The Agricultural Stabilization Act is financed entirely by tax dollars, whereas the Western Grain Stabilization Act is financed presumably one-third by producer levy and two-thirds by the Government. One of the myths that was shattered concerned this whole funding business, that it should always be and will always be on a three to one basis. That myth was shattered in committee when we started hearing from expert witnesses and began looking at the record. We know that close to $1 billion has been accumulated in the fund, taking into account producer pay-outs and the Government's share. Since its inception in 1976 there have been two payouts. Something like $122 million was paid out in 1977 and an additional $293 million was paid out in 1978. We are expect-
June 27, 1984

ing a pay-out in the order of $250 million to $300 million with this one. Farmers have participated in this particular program with the understanding and expectation that for every dollar they contributed some day in the future when they get into trouble they would be able to recoup $3.
We looked at the expert testimony and went through some of the numbers which had been generated by an economist from the Department of Agriculture in Manitoba. We went back 18 years using real data. Using the old five-year formula we found that for the 6 per cent collected of producer and federal Government money together, the potential pay-out over the full 18 years would have been 2.84 per cent. Not quite half of the moneys collected as premiums would be paid out in a period of 18 years. That pay-out procedure improves only slightly with the new improved formula which this Bill is attempting to introduce. Using the same data of the last 18 years and assuming contributions of one-third by the producer and two-thirds by the federal Government for a total input of 6 per cent, the total pay-out would be 4 per cent. The expectation among producers was that for every dollar put in they would eventually collect $3. However, the reality is that even with the new improved formula, for every dollar put in they are only able to collect $2.
The formula and calculation of the premium has been done on an extremely conservative basis. It is not designed to provide the kind of income protection that farmers had expected. The pay-out is always going to be much less than the expectation. For that reason we were a bit unhappy that major changes to the Bill had not resulted from a full review of the Act. It has been in effect for eight years and the past fall and winter would have been an excellent time to have done a complete review. We could have looked at the obvious shortcomings in the Bill, turned it over to the committee, and allowed it to come up with a much more comprehensive program which would have gone some way toward providing some income insurance protection to farmers. The fund which has been built up could have been used in a way which would provide real dollars in farmers' pockets when their income is down, due to low prices or bad markets. I am really sorry that that did not happen. However, since we are up against a time limit at this stage, we are prepared to allow the Government to put the amendments forward to trigger a pay-out so that this money will get into farmers' hands before the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to the House tonight on this very important legislation. I must begin by expressing the disappointment of my own constituents which I have heard reiterated over and over again since my entry into politics some 14 months ago. When I began to campaign about 14 months ago, one of the things of which I became immediately aware was how bitter the farmers in my constituency were about the inadequacies of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. By and large the farmers I talked to during the course of this time were of one mind. They said two things. They said
Western Grain Stabilization Act that this program had failed to do what it purported to do; it had failed to stabilize the industry. They had very little difficulty convincing me of that because the bankruptcy figures speak tragically for themselves. As you know, they have risen to near record levels year by year since 1979.
They also told me that most of them would prefer to be permitted to leave the program if they were able to recover the money which they themselves had invested. Of course, they were denied that opportunity. Although the amendments will now permit them to leave on the tenth anniversary of the program, they will, of course, have to leave without recovering the contributions which they made. By and large, the western Canadian farmers which I am acquainted with have been exceedingly disappointed by this legislation.
We now have before us amendments which come far too late and do too little. However, in some ways it is like the saying that a half a loaf is better than none. While we on this side of the House are disappointed that the Government failed to take the opportunity which was before it to perfect this legislation so that it would do what it purported to do, we are in a position where we must support the legislation if only because it is a step in the right direction. I would hope that we will be given the opportunity to again amend this legislation in the not too distant future. We hope to be able to take the opportunity to reform it in such a way as to make it truly responsive to the needs of western Canadian agriculture with sufficient flexibility to meet the year by year needs of cash starved Canadian grain farmers.
Farmers are now saying to me, with obvious justification, that the Government has betrayed them in that they are receiving only what they themselves contributed. As you know, western Canadian grain farmers have contributed almost exactly the amount of money which will now be involved in the interim payment to be made in July and the final payment to be made later in the autumn. Those farmers ask what has happened to the Government's contribution. They are critical of the amendments, with just cause.
However, thanks to the amendments and to the pressure which has been put on the Government by the Conservative opposition and the organizations which represent farmers across the country, the Bill is better now than when it was introduced into the House some time ago. There will at least be a very necessary interim payment toward the end of July. That interim payment is of the utmost importance. Farmers desperately need to augment their cash flow during the first few months of the year. That has always been a problem with western Canadian agriculture. There is a reasonable amount of cash flow in the autumn of the year at harvest time, but there is a serious shortage of funds in the spring of the year.
We have hoped that our amendments would be accepted. Those amendments would have provided for an interim payment in each and every year in which there was to be a pay-out. Unfortunately, the Government has seen fit to deal with this year only on an ad hoc basis. We are grateful for the concessions which the Government has made, but we regret that it failed to take the opportunity to redress a serious

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act grievance which has existed. I am also disappointed, as are my colleagues, that the Government failed to take the opportunity to make the changes retroactive. Had the Government made the proposed changes retroactive to the 1982-83 crop year, we could have generated at least another $100 million into the western Canadian grain economy. That would have assisted those farmers very substantially. Many of those farmers are very young and are on the verge of bankruptcy.
The situation in agriculture in western Canada today is very serious. I speaker of western Canada because I know it best. There are many young farmers who will not survive this fall unless we have an exceptionally good crop. If it is only an average crop, many of those farmers will tragically be forced into bankruptcy. They request us to provide them with whatever assistance is available because they need it. In fact, they need a real stabilization program.
One of the characteristics of the agricultural economy is that it tends to have serious ups and downs. As legislators, we must take steps to even out those returns in such a way that there can be some stability in the industry. We will need those farmers and their productivity in the future. If we fail them in their moment of need and they are forced off the land because of the current crisis, then they will not be producing at a time when Canada and the western world needs their food products.
What is needed is a genuine stabilization program, one which will address itself to the price that farmers receive for their product, and one which will address itself to the cost of their production. Unfortunately, the present program has failed to fulfil either of those two objectives. It has not dealt adequately with the price that the farmer receives for his product each year, and has not taken into consideration all of his costs of production. Because of the increased volume which has affected the value of the over-all crop and has ignored the question of the cost of production, there has been an inadequate response on the part of this program to the needs of western Canadian agriculture.
While the Government has moved in the right direction, unfortunately, as the Government has done so often, it has taken only half a step. I am not sure if this is because it is excessively cautious or that it lacks concern. It has taken a step in the right direction but it has failed to respond in the manner in which western Canadian farmers have asked.
We need a program which is more flexible. I submit that a program which use three-year averages rather than five-year averages would be more flexible and would meet the needs of the western Canadian agriculture better than it now does. We need a program in which there is ample opportunity, whenever the need is there, to introduce the interim payment rather than deal with it in an ad hoc manner. I cannot help but regret that this program did not take those necessary steps forward. I cannot help but regret that this program did not take into account the poor crop years of 1982 and 1983.
What we have before us is something which is better than nothing. Constituents have said to me that we in the Opposition should oppose this legislation because of its inadequacy. They wanted us to vote against it. They wanted us to fight it every step of the way. I understand the frustration of those farmers, but what they are asking us to do is not practical, because this Bill is better than nothing. Unfortunately, it is not nearly enough. It may well be, and in fact appears to be, that we will have to wait until the next election and the next Conservative Government in order to get the kind of legislation which western Canadian farmers so desperately need.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words about this Bill, which will be given third reading tonight and become law at the end of this Session of Parliament. It has taken a long time. We on this side have been pressing for amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Bill for the last two or three years. We realize that the Bill itself is not an effective means of stabilizing the income of western farmers.
I was interested in the Minister's remarks this evening. His speech was rather good until the end when he began setting forth the various government programs which he indicated had been helpful to the farmers of western Canada. It sounded to me as though he was making a speech in anticipation of an election which we expect to come very shortly. However, the Minister did not tell the people of Canada that the programs he was talking about are programs which are funded with taxpayers' money, not government money. The $250 million or $300 million that will be paid out under this Bill will be welcome in western Canada. However, I suggest that it will not do the job.
It is a great government.

The Hon. Member across the way says that it is a great government. We will see after the next election whether the public feels that you have a great government. I doubt very much that they will.
As I said before I was interrupted, that $300 million will be welcome in western Canada. I repeat that it will not do the job because it will be an average of approximately $2,500 to each producer. That money will come out of a fund that is close to $1 billion. The $300 million is simply a return of the contributions that the farmers have made over the years and does not give them a return of interest on their money.
For the last several years, as I travelled throughout my constituency, almost without exception the farmers asked me why they cannot opt out of this program. I told them that they are locked in. I am pleased to see that there is an amendment which provides for a ten-year opting out clause. It will be interesting to see what effect this will have on the producers. Unless there are more changes to this Bill I suspect that there will be an increasing number of producers opting out of this program.
Farmers in western Canada are in serious financial difficulty. Their input costs have been rising; their cost of fuel under this Government has more than doubled. The cost of fertilizer has been rising as a result of the National Energy Program.
June 27, 1984

Furthermore, machinery prices have doubled and tripled and interest rates continue to go up to the extent that many farmers are finding it almost impossible to meet the interest payments on the loans they have with the banks or the Farm Credit Corporation.
It is interesting to note that recently a farmer came to my office to talk about his Farm Credit Corporation loan. He was unable to meet his payments last year and, lo and behold, a few weeks ago a representative from the Farm Credit Corporation came to him and said, "You are in arrears. We want to take a statement of your assets because we are considering taking foreclosure action." This man was worried and told me that he had put in his crop and that if it rains, and it has since, he will have a reasonably good crop and will hopefully be able to meet his commitments. He wanted to know how fast they could take his farm. I said, "First, the legal procedure in foreclosing is a fairly lengthy process". I also told him that there will be a payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Program. While it will not be very large, there is an election in the offing and I also suspect that just prior to the election there will be an interim payment by the Wheat Board. I told this farmer that if he added those two payments he would probably be able to pay a substantial amount of the arrears to the Farm Credit Corporation and they will get off his back. I certainly expect that prior to the election there will be an interim payment and another payment on account of the final payment on the grain sales.
The problems faced by farmers also become the problems of the small businessman in the communities, such as the implement dealer, the fuel dealer and the fertilizer dealer. If the farmer does not have the money and is unable to get money to pay his operating expenses, the small businessman is also affected. You will find bankruptcies occurring among small business people.
The Minister talked about this Bill as one to stabilize farm income or to help the farmer. But really it is not such a Bill. The Bill is simply one to put money into the economy of western Canada without regard for the individual producer. The Minister said that the amendments will make this Bill sensitive and flexible. It will make some changes, but it will not make it a Bill satisfactory to the farmers of western Canada. When the original Bill was before the House and before the committee we on this side of the House told the then Minister that the plan would not work in a satisfactory manner. First we said it was a global plan and anyone who has any knowledge of agriculture in western Canada knows that year in and year out the whole of the Canadian Wheat Board area does not have a good crop. You have areas, sometimes large, where the crop is poor. We have an area in northeast Saskatchewan today where there has not been a crop for three years, and the Western Grain Stabilization program has not helped the farmers in that area. Even on a regional basis, Mr. Speaker, it would not serve the purpose. Some of us who served on the committee in 1973-74 recalled that we had participated in the old Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and know
Western Grain Stabilization Act
it did not function. If Members on the other side or the Minister would refer to the committee hearings, they would note that we on this side of the House made several proposals whereby the Bill could be made to function on an individual basis without any particular complications. But the then Minister, Mr. Otto Lang, would not listen to us. He said in the debates and in the committee: "We will pay out in the spring of the year." That money has never been paid out in the spring. He said it was important that the farmers have the money in the spring so they could put in their crops. That has not happened. We gave him a solution, but he did not listen to us.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling to me that my time has just about run out. In closing, let me say that it is vital that the Bill itself, the concept of grain stabilization, agriculture stabilization, should be examined and examined in detail with the provinces. I would suggest that after the next election when there is a new Progressive Conservative Government that that examination and those changes will take place.
Hear, hear!
