speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
For debate, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger).

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
Mr. Speaker, the Crees of the Peace Hills will wonder about your pronunciation, but many people have trouble with the name of my riding.
Hear, hear!

I am pleased to join in the debate on the Western Grain Stabilization Act. As farmers contemplate the crop year-they have just planted their crops incidentally-the indications are that it is going to be another tough year. The only opportunities for them seem to lie in the possibility of one country or another in the world having a crop failure which would boost the prices of grains. That is a tragic situation that farmers have to hope for in order to get more farm income.
At one time many farms were much smaller than they are today. At one time the farmer as he was farming, producing a crop and selling it, could anticipate a reasonable profit, and along with it he had the opportunity to put some of that money into a savings account, now called a stabilization account. In those days there were no such things as stabilization or crop insurance. The farmer had to put aside part of his income to make sure that if he suffered adverse weather conditions, whether it was drought or too much rain, he had the capacity to deal with it. But now in modern times when farm equipment has become very expensive the price for produce versus the cost of putting the grain in the ground has forced farmers to go to bigger farms, to produce higher volumes in order to survive, because volume is the only basis upon which they can continue the farm and buy equipment. We are now as governments, both provincial and federal, forced to assist in the setting up of stabilization accounts. This was not the case in the past. Farmers stabilized their own income. They were able to do that.
Now as farmers contemplate their abilities, they have only three bases upon which to continue to farm. They can hope that prices for their produce will increase enabling them to continue to farm. First, they have to get the price of their produce up or the cost to produce down. Because we sell on the international market it is difficult to get the price up. For some commodities that are controlled by supply management boards that is a situation that can be altered domestically, but most of our produce, particularly western grain, is sold on the international market and that is not the case. There is not a lot of room for farmers to get the price for their produce up.
The other option of getting the cost down is one where the Government can effect the situation. We have talked about things on this side, such as interest rate reduction, agri-bonds and farm fuel decreases, and I could go on to mention other bases upon which we can get the cost down.
Then there are the stabilization programs. This is one of them and there are others. We have talked about a Bill which the Government just introduced for a beef stabilization program where there will be three participants. Another way is for more international agreements under which we would guarantee our markets into the future. We could have something like the two-price wheat agreement where the domestic
market pays more for the consumption of domestic food in order to assist farmers in the export of their produce. We are now faced with one of those programs, the Western Grain Stabilization Program. We are attempting to make things better for the farmers of Western Canada.
As my colleagues have said, this is not an individual plan. It was intended to be a plan to stabilize prairie income, most of which is derived from the farming community, particularly in Saskatchewan. It is also a very important part of the Alberta and Manitoba economies. The rural communities in which many of us grew up are changing rapidly. The main reason for that is that farmers are no longer able to buy most of their necessities in small communities. The community dealers cannot compete with large machinery dealers and large hardware stores for the types of goods farmers require. As a result, in many parts of the Prairies small communities are having great difficulty surviving.
This Bill was intended to assist in that survival. It was to put money in the hands of farmers at a time when the total economy of the Prairies was in a recession. While we had some difficulty with the Act, it was passed in 1976. It worked reasonably well until factors such as volume of grain exported, inflation, interest rates and so forth, changed in the late seventies and early eighties. The Bill was no longer functioning properly, so amendments were brought forth. We welcomed those amendments.
Also, as my colleagues have indicated, across the Prairies it was seen as the only piece of legislation or the only fund of money upon which farmers could get their hands to put their crops in the ground and survive this year. The indications from the Canadian Wheat Board were that the initial price would be lower, not higher. Of course farmers had to have crops before they could receive advance payments. Their only opportunity to put crops in the ground this year, other than by borrowing money on the backs of fertilizer and fuel dealers, was the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. However, we did not get the Bill through in time. Because of that I assume many accounts are being carried by small businesses in western Canadian communities today. That is the only reason many grain farmers are still in production.
This interim payment is very welcome across western Canada. This is why I found it difficult to understand why the Government, when it brought in an amendment allowing an interim payment this year, restricted the interim payment to only this year. I know the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board said that farmers need money in the fall just as they do in the spring. Anyone in the House who farms knows that one's opportunity for cash is much greater when a crop has been harvested than when it is planted. Planting is the most expensive of the farming processes. Therefore an interim payment, if it is to be made, should be made in time for farmers to pay their planting bills. Not much interest would be involved in order to obtain an interim payment in July.
June 27, 1984

I certainly agree with the other amendments, but the point I am making is that the interim payment should not be restricted to this year. It ought to be available in future years if there is to be a payment under this plan. That is a serious deficiency. At a time when we have opened up this Act, we should not close it and leave it closed in this fashion. I ask the Government to reconsider this. I know it is too late at this stage, and I think that is a failure. How could the Minister stand to speak on the Bill and brag about some of the other things he is doing with taxpayers' money in western Canada, such as the Crow Bill? I hope he campaigns on that in the next election in western Canada. We will see what happens.

Mr. Speaker, you may or
may not know that a west wind is blowing and that there is a strong odour of an election in the air. Jimmy Carter has risen again. The Government has a new set of twisted mirrors with which to persuade farmers that their own money is a gift from Lloyd's of Winnipeg and the keeper of the western gate to Gritsville. The boom and bust cycle has become bust, bust, bust, election year boom; bust, bust, bust, election year boom. This is what Lloyd's of Winnipeg is offering farmers with their own money.
Confidence has gone. Unfortunately-and I could dwell on it for some time-if farmers had a real and honest free choice to get back the money invested in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund and get out, the majority would do so today. It is not the concept of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund which is wrong, but confidence has been destroyed. Farmers no longer believe in the program. Moreover and equally dangerous, that destroyed confidence or lack of confidence is spilling over into any other concept of stabilization. If we ask farmers and ranchers in my riding about whether or not they want a red meat stabilization plan, they will say that they do not want it. Whether intellectually or academically a good and workable idea, it is set aside. The response of those people is to say: "If it is like the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, I want no part of it".
We used to have stabilization funds in the 1930s, and beyond. They were called chickens, pigs, milk cows, gardens, Saskatoon berries and the muscle power of animals and humans. Once farms were paid for, farms with low capital costs and subject to low interest rates, a farmer could not be starved off the land. He could feed and look after his family. Today input costs are so high that they can no longer afford crop losses. Persons farming today who have virtually paid for everything can be destroyed by two crop losses.
At the present time the Prairies of northeastern Saskatchewan have faced crop failure. Major parts of Manitoba are into their third year of crop failure. We see farmers going bankrupt, not at the Prairies average which is already too high, but at regional averages which are excessive to the extreme. As long as the pay-out is based upon the whole area of the Canadian Wheat Board it will be merely a stabilization of the machinery manufacturing businesses and fertilizer plants of central Canada.
Western Grain Stabilization Act
These people propel a certain amount of business into the Prairies year after year. Now they have a guarantee. If the whole Prairies went broke, machinery dealers and manufacturers would be able to market in the Prairies. That is really what the plan is all about, unfortunately. Every small region of the Prairies at one time or another experiences crop failure. It shifts around from one region to another. Some years the Peace River country of Alberta is frozen over. This year northeastern Saskatchewan will be rained out. Surely they should be able to stabilize their farms, not the manufacturing industry of some other region of Canada.
The Government is gasping for breath at the eleventh hour and fifty-ninth minute before the election call. Well after seeding has been completed, it comes along and tells farmers that it will give them back their own money which they paid into the fund. The truth of the matter is that had farmers invested their money when the fund was initially conceived, even at bank interest rates, they would have been about $8,000 better off than by investing in the fund.
As the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) just mentioned, when a farmer plants seed in the ground he cannot go to the bank and ask for a loan to carry him over on the basis of there being seed in the good earth. But when there is a 50 or 60-bushel crop lying in swath, the farmer can make projections because the predictability of cash is much better than it was in the spring of the year. They need the money in the spring. As the Minister said, they have expenses in the fall as well, but they are much closer to predicting what their income might be.
Last weekend I met with a farmer who told me that he argued in favour of the Liberal Government when this program was initiated. He said: "I argued with my neighbours that any time that I as a farmer could put up $1 and the Government would put up $2, that was a deal I could not afford to pass up." He went on to state: "Boy, was I dead wrong. I feel damn cheated." He did go on to say some other words. Because I want to continue my speech for some time, I will not put them into Hansard.
This Government has chosen to stabilize the farmer when he is broke. It is not the notion of what grain stabilization is about at all. We recognize that there are ups and downs in the income of farm people. They waited until the very last breath of farmers and decided at that point to come in with stabilization. Coming in then basically means that we continue the path of bankruptcy for all too many farmers.
The present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has been Minister for 12 years. In that time there have been five major pieces of agricultural legislation. That is a record that damns this Government in terms of its agriculture policy. There is no industry in the world as important as agriculture. Every year 70 million persons suffer permanent and irreversible brain damage from the lack of protein; four-fifths of this world suffers from malnutrition and 40,000 children under the age of five die of starvation. There is no commodity in the world as

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
important as food. There are only two sources of food. One is soil and the other is water. Unfortunately, and I do not blame only the Liberals who govern us, against that devastating background, there is no nation in the world that places fish, forestry or food among its highest priorities for government spending. The whole world needs to turn itself around to recognize that we live by the good earth. If we do not put some research, marketing, development and skills back into the production of foods, we will continue as we have in the past, living in a world where four-fifths of our people suffer from malnutrition.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) took the occasion this evening to tell us that the West should be pretty happy because we have this great thing he calls the new Crow rate. We got exactly what we should have expected. We have Senator Ian Sinclair in the other place. He is now part of this great new Government team. We have a new Leader of the Liberal Party. He did not dare resign his directorship of CP. A good constituent, of mine, the Hon. Jack Horner, the former Chairman of CNR, is now the western grain car co-ordinator. If I was a farmer against that background I would hightail it like a jack-rabbit.
It is those people who gave us exactly what we should expect, a Crow rate that allows the railway companies to renege on about $2 billion which they said they would spend. They are not going to spend that because somehow it is not in the interest of the railway. This country is not about railways. It is about people who produce, whether it is forestry, fish or agriculture. When we have people like Sinclair, Turner and Horner looking after farmers, it is analogous to sending a tomcat to guard mice. They will look after the railways every time.
We have to recognize that we face a $2 billion shortfall. That is against the background of a 140 per cent increase in farm production in the last decade. Statistics Canada predicts another 110 per cent increase by the end of the year 1986. We tax fuels used by the farmers. We have front-end taxes on natural gas which makes fertilizer prices too high. Land prices are escalating far too high. We have machinery costs that cannot be justified. Interest rates are too high. They are exorbitant, and there is no means of resolving the situation. There is a failure in marketing and research in terms of farm production and agricultural needs. Against that background, there was one committee meeting at which the Liberals did not show up. At the other meeting, one Liberal Member showed up and he walked out.
The Government left this measure until the second last day before the recess. It brings in this Bill at the last second, 11 hours, 59 minutes and 59 seconds. It tries to tell the farmers it is going to give them some gift from Lloyds of Winnipeg at the last moment with the farmers' own money.
I know this is a good speech, Mr. Speaker, but you do not have to come down here. I will keep going if I can do so. No? If that is the signal, I will resume my seat. Thank you very much.

Mr. Speaker, I sat through virtually every committee meeting when this Bill was being considered. From day one, its primary purpose was not to come to the aid of the farmer. Its primary purpose, and it is so stated in the Bill and in the Minister's presentation, and in its support by Government, was to make sure that there was a total income in the West, including all industries and not just agriculture, so as to maintain a healthy western economy. As a result, the provisions of this Bill are not properly triggered at the time when farm income declines to the point perceived by farmers are the one described by the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) a few moments ago. It was perceived by the farmers as their Bill. It was utterly and totally impossible to indicate to the public at large that this was not to be triggered by farm needs, but rather the total economic needs of the total western area. The farmer now realizes that he was utterly and totally misled by the propaganda associated with the presentation of that Bill.
We now find ourselves considering an amendment which is vital to the farm industry of western Canada. It is high time that it was here. This Bill was needed when people were planting crops so there would be an attraction to plant, and encouragement for farmers and creditors alike to ensure a healthy plant and healthy agriculture in western Canada.
This is the first recognition of the weakness of the original Bill that we are amending, the first recognition of its weakness as it is being presented for amendment today. I do not know how farmers in Canada can ever be bewitched again into a state of ignorance of their own affairs and the legislation which was supposed to attack the problems they face.
We have gone through a period of time when costs of production have skyrocketed. Price stabilization, whether it be for western grains or other items, is something which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has refused to recognize. He has preached a cheap food policy for Canada. As he preached that, net farm income has gone down and costs have gone up. There have been all kinds of presentations to this House; to the Minister, to the Cabinet and to Opposition Parties, pleading for recognition of the problem of the red meat industry and the horticulture industry. They suggest that the policy of this Government has not been adequate to look after the farmers' needs while the Cabinet and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) preach that we shall have cheap food for Canada. The birds are just coming home to roost by this Bill.
What the Opposition Parties said when it was in the process of consideration by the Committee in the House has now been admitted by the Government. It was inadequate the day it was drafted. It was not subject to amendment like most government Bills. Government Members had all the brains. They bewitched the farmers and passed the Bill as it was when amendments had been offered to try to have payment triggered by farm needs rather than total economic needs. That, of course, was a reversal of the situation.
June 27, 1984

If one follows the economic charts of Canada through history, one sees that when the farm industry is prosperous, so is the rest of Canada. There are a few exceptions to that rule, being times when the peaks do not entirely coincide, but there are no times when the impact of farm prosperity is not reflected into the curve of prosperity for all of Canada. The decline of the agricultural economy may precede the decline of the Canadian economy, but then one wonders whether or not the agricultural economy has dragged the entire economy down.
Here we are considering this Bill after hearing a snide remark made by a Member on your right, Mr. Speaker, a remark which was intended to be deceptive after mention was made of the 18 cents. How many times must one tell those who will not hear-I suppose one can tell them in perpetuity and they will still not hear-that the 18 cents did not apply to agriculture, to fishing or to the heating of homes. Remarks such as that do not do the dignity of this House very much justice.
I regret very much that, as of now, we have not properly addressed at least a few of the agricultural problems. I do not have to name those problems because the Minister of Agriculture himself receivd a telex urging a response to the request of the Canadian Horticultural Council. This response was not mentioned as the business for tomorrow, nor was it promised as the business for Friday. I must say that this would be a default in the responsibility of any Government. This is a position about which we have known for weeks and for which no correcting legislation has been presented to us as of yet.
As was mentioned earlier, it seems as though the ghost of Jimmie Gardiner has finally injected his thinking into the policy of a Government that is just about to attack the public with an election campaign. The same tactics are being applied, but this time the farmers will not have their eyes shut because there have been too many examples of neglect and too few examples of progressive, constructive, promotional legislation for the welfare of agriculture in all its spheres. This is just a hypocritical example of the historic neglect which has been going on for too many years.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be afforded the opportunity to say a few words on this Bill tonight because my constituency is largely agricultural. There are some excellent tourist areas such as Lake Louise, Banff, Drumheller and a few other places in my constituency, but the vast number of people who live in the constituency of Bow River either depend directly or indirectly upon agriculture for their living. There is a great deal of ranching and livestock production and there is a tremendous amount of grain growing that goes on in the Bow River area. Consequently, this Bill is very important to the livelihood of the people of my constituency.
I wish to deal with some of the fundamentals first. I wonder why it is that agriculture and farmers, to put it colloquially, always get the dirty end of the stick. That is what has
Western Grain Stabilization Act happened over the years. Agriculture never gets a fair break. I have thought about this and wondered why this is so. The agricultural industry is basic to our entire lives. If we do not eat, we do not live. We do not eat unless there is production and production comes largely from our farms. Almost everything we eat comes from the land or from the sea. Farmers have a tremendous part to play in the production of the food that keeps us alive. So why is it that the agricultural industry always seems to be lagging behind the rest of the economy?
As the Hon. Member who just spoke said a few moments ago, when the farmers have money and are reasonably prosperous, the entire community is buoyant. I have seen that happen many, many times. I have seen times when our coal mines were working full blast, and that brought prosperity and buoyancy to the entire area around the coal mines. I have seen times when our farmers were getting a fairly reasonable price for their produce, and that brought buoyancy to the entire area. Consequently, it is important to analyse the situation and find out why farming has never been given its proper place.
The situation is like that of the Government's job programs. Every time a question is asked, the Ministers stand and say that we spent so many millions on this, so many billions on that. Government members are throwing money at jobs and they think the money, like an aspirin, will find the sore spot and cure it. Money does not work that way, and that is why the more millions of dollars that are spent, the more unemployment goes up.
If the Government were to diagnose the problem and find out what is causing unemployment-and the Government itself is causing it with things like the capital cost allowance- and then try to find solutions to those particular problems, it would be attacking things in a logical and scientific way. However, the Government does not do that. Government members just say that they are spending so many million dollars and they think that that satisfies the problem, even if the rate of unemployment keeps increasing as it does. The same is true with farmers.
Tonight the Government is saying that it is giving $300 million to the farmers. In the first place, it is the farmers' own money. The Government should stop arguing about the ratio of three to one. That stabilization fund was brought in so that the money contributed to it by the farmers and the money contributed to it by the Government would belong to the farmers. All of that money belongs to the farmers. That was the deal that the Government made with the agricultural community. Now it is telling the farmers that it is giving them two for one. By law and by agreement, every dollar in that stabilization fund belongs to the farmers. I do not like the Government now beginning to change that agreement and divide it up.
Let us look at the situation. Each part of the economy depends on every other part of the economy. Each part of the economy must be in proper balance for the economy as a whole to work. I think that is an important point. Basically, this means that the price received by one sector for its production must fit properly with the price received by other sectors.

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act There must be a proper balance between the prices. When that proper balance exists among all of the sectors, including the agricultural sector, then there is parity.
Farmers have been asking for parity for a long time. Parity simply means that there is a proper balance between the various parts of the economy, including the agricultural sector. If one sector charges prices that are too high, then it exists at the expense of the other sectors. If one sector receives too little for its production as farmers normally do, then it becomes the victim of the other sectors. If one sector borrows to the hilt, that too hurts the agricultural sector.
Producers have been the victims of our economy. Of the entire national income of Canada, 14 per cent should go to the agricultural sector. However, it is very seldom that the agricultural sector receives even close to that amount. There is no parity. Farmers do not get their fair share of the national production. As a matter of fact, probably the closest farmers have ever come to getting a fair share happened shortly after the war when farm produce was receiving a half-decent price.
Normally farmers receive an amount way below the national production and sometimes receive only 1 per cent, 2 per cent or 3 per cent of the national production. Consequently, they cannot exist. These low incomes create problems for more people than the farmers. The income that was not received by farmers fails to spread throughout the rest of the economy. When farmers do receive money, the benefits are spread throughout the rest of the economy. When the farmers do not receive it, their share of national production is way down.
In such times what do farmers have to do? They have to borrow. This starts that wicked cycle all over again-the farmer gets into debt and things get worse. High interest rates have hurt farmers and home owners more than anybody else. People produce with credit. Farmers need credit to produce. It is no wonder that 400 farmers went bankrupt in western Canada in 1983. Many more farmers went bankrupt across Canada because they could not meet their costs.
The Farm Credit Corporation and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) tell those farmers that they should sell some of their land. Farmers paid into the stabilization fund in the hope that when bad times came they would receive a little help with the money which they put into the fund. That is not the case. PC Members have begged, pleaded and prayed for the Government to make pay-outs. Month after month the Minister of Agriculture said, "soon". The Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) told us that the Government was studying the legislation. It was studied for months, and in the meantime farmer after farmer went bankrupt. The money which was in that fund could have saved scores of those farmers if the Government had acted.
Why did it not act? It did not act for a very simple reason: The fund did not cover total costs. The program is spread over half the country. As well, it covers a number of products. Some farmers have no hope in the world of ever receiving a pay-out. About the only thing which will trigger a pay-out is
the wheat of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. All the other producers will probably never see a pay-out. We asked the Government to include the total costs of production. The Government has improved the legislation somewhat, but it still does not include all of the costs of production.
What about the interest costs? That is one of the biggest costs of agriculture. That is not included. What about inflationary prices? They are not included. What about the costs of transportation? That is a factor in production. What about the costs of machinery? Oh, no, the Government leaves out the important things.
I am glad to see this Bill. At least it will give farmers something to put in their pockets. It will give back to the farmers some of their own money. However, this Bill is still unfair. There will be farmers who put money into this fund who will never get back a cent. These farmers are being robbed by the Government. When these farmers opt out, if they have not received as much or more than they put in, plus interest and plus the contribution by the Government, they should be paid the difference. If they did not receive any pay-out at all, they should get their money back with interest.
Hear, hear!

Absolutely. Any other business in the world would do that. It is highway robbery. The Minister can laugh if he likes, but the farmers are not laughing. The Government takes their money year after year after year and then we in the Opposition have to beg the Government to give those farmers a little bit back-a few crumbs so that they can stay alive. It almost seems that the Government is trying to bankrupt the farms.

subtopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS PRESENTATION OF SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS PRESENTATION OF SIXTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the implication of the Hon. Member who spoke last is one that I cannot refuse. I appreciate very much the consent of the House in allowing me to rise to present the Sixth Report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I thank the House very much for the privilege it has accorded me.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-33, An Act to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Agriculture; and the amendment (Mr. Axworthy).

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is before the House of Commons at a time when Canadian farmers are in trouble. They are in trouble for a number of reasons. Part of the problem in my province might have been due to the weather in the spring of 1984, and the weather which we have experienced over the past few weeks, namely, excessive rain. But, farmers throughout the ages who have followed the pursuits of farming, the production of food, have always been able to cope with that kind of trouble. What is causing more farming bankruptcies today is not due to the weather, it is due to government policy.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone), mentioned, the Bill before us will be passed in the last minutes of this House before it rises for the summer, and possibly the end of this Parliament should an election intervene. It is a Bill which is, at best, a minimal attempt to address the issues which farmers in Canada are facing. What farmers are facing, Mr. Speaker, is a debt load and an increasing interest rate problem which is jeopardizing their economic viability more than any other single factor.
This weekend, before I came back to Ottawa, a young farmer in my riding called me. I know him very well. He is farming with his father and they have a successful farm. He asked me whether or not the Western Grain Stabilization Bill would be passed before the House rose for the summer. I told him that from our point of view, we not only had asked for the Bill, but through the weeks we had pressured the Government for the Bill, and that we would do everything in our power to see the Bill passed before the end of June. At that point in the conversation I asked him if it would make a great deal of difference in their farming operations. He said to me, "It is not going to solve our problems but anything which will in some way address the financial squeeze we are in is welcome". That, Mr. Speaker, is why we have pushed for this Bill.
I want to tell the House that this Bill does not resolve or solve the financial problems of the farming community today. I have already said that the major problem is the financing of the debt load. That is why farmers are going bankrupt. That is why we are seeing foreclosures. That is why we are seeing unrest on the Prairies, for example, among people who, when they produce food, are at their best. When you look at the economic history of Canada over any period, but especially the post-war period, there has been no group of people in society who have been more efficient and whose productivity has

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act
increased more dramatically than the farmers, and it is because of that that they are still surviving.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, if one takes a look at the more traditional industries, what some people would like to call the multinationals, one will find that with respect to their postwar labour situation, on a net basis they have not created new jobs. They have stabilized their labour force, and in most cases their labour force is down. There are three areas in which the labour force has been increased. One area is the public service, which has had tremendous growth over this period of time. The other two areas are small business and agriculture. We cannot even measure what the effect on the labour force is when agriculture is doing well or is not doing well.
Many years ago I was working in a small business in my home community which sold cars and trucks for General Motors. It is very interesting to note that in Ontario at that time the automobile manufacturers felt they had a good year when the economy was growing. They had an excellent year when farmers would come in at the tail end of the tax year and put in orders for trucks, cars and machinery. It is no different on the Prairies today. They are shrewd business people. I say to you that agriculture is the industry which creates jobs, and today part of our labour problems are due to the financial squeeze which our agriculture communities are in.
We now have the stabilization bill before us. On average this Bill will give $2,500 to farmers who will simply be getting the money back which they put into the fund in the first place. I do not know if you know this, Mr. Speaker, but I know that there are some of my colleagues in this House-and I will not identify them-along with farmers in my riding, who will spend more money today in spraying their crops than the average pay-out from the grain stabilization is going to give them. That is the situation. There is no point, Mr. Speaker, in saying in this House of Commons today that this legislation is going to do wonders for the farm economy. It is only of minimal help, but thank goodness, at least there is something.
I remember when this Act was passed. At that time, a former Hon. Member for Assiniboia, now the Leader of the Liberal Party of Saskatchewan, was working with the then Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, the Hon. Otto Lang. I remember him running up and down the aisles of this House trying to convince us from western Canada that this would be a good deal for western farmers. I will never forget it. I remember him going back and forth trying to get the deal put together. We consistently asked him what guarantee will the farmers have? Where is the commitment from the Government? But he was absolutely convinced that this was the best thing which would ever happen to western agriculture. What is ironic is that this Government, which passed that legislation, today, last week and last month, has been forced, pushed and cajoled into bringing forward legislation which would at least reflect in part the economic reality that is now facing western Canada. The Western Grain Stabilization Act was simply not realistic.
It is important to note today what we said then when that Bill was passed. We said that those clauses were of such a
nature there literally had to be a disaster if there was going to be a pay-out. It was not the Government which was taking a risk. It was the farmer who was putting the money into the fund who was taking the total risk. That is what we were dealing with. And all we are doing today, Mr. Speaker, is correcting in part, in a small way, what was wrong in the first place.
I want this Bill to be passed today, but I want notice to be served that I am not impressed with this Bill. Nor am I impressed with the government's agricultural policy. It takes more to give leadership in agriculture than to walk around the country wearing a green stetson. If we are going to get this country turned around economically we must get back to the basics, such as agriculture. There has to be more emphasis placed on agriculture. In the 12 years I have been here, Mr. Speaker, this Government has brought forward few bills relating to agriculture. More importantly, agriculture has not been a priority of the Cabinet. Some of my colleagues might disagree with my next statement, but a least sometimes I thought the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was trying to give some voice to agriculture, but it fell on the deaf ears of his colleagues.
All we are doing today, Mr. Speaker, is correcting in part that which was wrong in the first place. What I am saying is that we have to place much more emphasis as Canadians on agriculture. If we will do that, not only will our agricultural community prosper but jobs across the country will be created. That lack of emphasis is the legacy of this Liberal Government. That is why its platitudes or sudden revelations that it knows where the West is finally located is not going to make any difference. The record speaks for itself and the agricultural record of this Government is something for which it should be condemned.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this debate. For a long, long time, I believe since before we broke at Christmas, Hon. Members of my Party have been asking the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) when the Western Grain Stabilization Bill would be brought into the real world and address the realities involved in farming in western Canada.
There is one day left before this House rises for the summer recess. In all likelihood we will be going into a general election. At least that is what we on this side are hoping for. But we have presented to us in the dying hours of this session a Bill that does not reflect the realities of the production of food. It does not reflect the realities of interest rates, the cost of fuel, machinery and fertilizer. Indeed, it does not reflect the realities involved in purchasing land or putting up farmstead buildings.
We on this side are going to support this Bill. I hear the Minister of Transport saying "good". I hope when the election is called he has the opportunity to come to my riding of Kindersley-Lloydminster in Saskatchewan. I invite him to
June 27, 1984

come and discuss with my farmers their feelings about the Western Grain Stabilization Act, indeed their feelings about the last 20 years of Liberal administration. I offer him the opportunity and we will see one another in Kindersley-Lloyd-minster in Saskatchewan.
Some $300 million is to be paid out under this Bill which the producers themselves have placed in trust with the Government of Canada so that it would be available to them when they needed it to stabilize their income. The Minister of Transport knows full well the amount of taxpayers' money, not farmers' money, which has been put into the riding of Win-nipeg-Fort Garry, his own riding, some $700 million to $800 million. The Minister is saying "yes, somewhere around there". He is not sure. That works out to $100,000 per voter. Now he is doing the math to see how much money he has spent on each one of the voters in his riding. He finds I have come up a little high.
Not much.

That is $700 million into one riding, and some 150,000 Wheat Board permit holders are being offered $300 million which the producers paid into the fund in the first place. The Government is offering to give it back, some $2,500 per farmer as estimated by the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board.
I am not a cynical man. I do not look for hidden motives or angles like some people on the other side of the House. But I am not sure, indeed I have great doubts, whether we would even be debating this Bill if there was not the possibility of a general election.
There is another thing which should be brought to the attention of the Minister. If the media reports are correct he is going to be-and I hate to say this because it refers to a native son of my province-another Jimmy Gardiner. He is now going to be responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. Woe to the producers of grain in western Canada if the Minister has that responsibility and is allowed to run amuck among the most sacred thing the producers of western Canada have, the only thing that protects them from the deviations of the world market, the Canadian Wheat Board.
We have noticed in the past that there seems to be a tendency on the part of this Government not to pay too much attention to the people who produced the grain, but to pay a lot of attention to the people who derive their livelihood on the backs of producers. A prime example would be Bill C-155, the transportation Bill, which the Minister of Transport brought in. After some debate and some amendments, he used closure to put it through the House. We have heard the estimates of the number of jobs being decreased and increased. It is now estimated at about 155,000 jobs, where before it was 300,000 plus. Think back to that debate. We heard about $16 billion being invested, but now it is only $12 billion. If you think back, we never once heard the railways give those numbers. We never heard them say there would be over 300,000 jobs created. They never said they would invest $16 billion. But I heard the Minister of Transport and his predecessors say it. I
Western Grain Stabilization Act read the expensive propaganda distributed throughout Canada saying that these investments would be made. But these statements were made by the Government, never by the railroads. Now we find that the railroads are not going to invest that money. But the Government used its propaganda machine to make people believe these investments would take place. I know the Minister of Transport is proud of being the co-campaign chairman for Mr. Turner who won the leadership of his Party. That is a political achievement, I am sure. Mr. Turner happened to be a director of Canadian Pacific.
Still is.

I am sure he was very close and comfortable with "Mr. six and five", Ian Sinclair. He now sits in the Senate, having been appointed by this Government.
Then there is that man who had his life reversed, Mr. Horner. Most people, if they are going to become a socialist, do so when they are young. Mr. Horner did it in reverse. He became a socialist Liberal when he got older. He is now the chairman of the Senior Grain Transportation Authority.
Then there was another Minister of Transport, the man who said, "Transportation is a mess but what will I do about it?" He went to the Senate and became Speaker. Then the present Minister of Transport had him appointed chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission.
Do you really think the grain producers in western Canada are being cynical, are being anything more than reasoned and rational people when they say "We really do not think we have a chance with this Government the way it stacks the deck for the Canadian Pacific Railroad". Does anyone wonder, given the Minister of Transport, the Leader of the Liberal Party, Senator Sinclair, Senator Marchand, now the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, and Mr. Horner, the chairman of the Senior Grain Transportation Authority?
Agriculture is a multimillion dollar industry, a megaproject which goes into the ground every year whether it is dry or wet. If farmers do not have the money, they borrow it. It is the biggest megaproject this country has and it is a renewable megaproject. It generates some $19 billion in Canada. Over half of that is generated on the Prairies. Right now costs have tripled since 1971. The prices received by producers are well below 1973 levels. There has to be some consideration for people who invest their lives and those of their families in the production of food. If there was, they could go ahead and do what they enjoy doing and contribute, not to just Canada but to the world. It does not make sense when we have the Farm Credit Corporation charging 15 per cent interest for farm loans, while at the same time this Government, through CIDA, gives some $44 million interest free to India for the production of forests. It does not make any sense. There has to be a happy medium.
I see I am keeping the Minister of Transport up. He looks tired. I know he has had a busy day, but the people out in Kindersley-Lloydminster, Provencher, Portage-Marquette, Crowfoot, Bow River, Wetaskiwin and Moose Jaw are just coming in from spraying. They have been spending money to

June 27, 1984
Western Grain Stabilization Act buy chemicals produced in another part of Canada. They get off a tractor that was built in another part of Canada. They get into a half-ton truck built in another part of Canada.
Don't you know about Versatile?

In 1967 I bought a Versatile tractor and the total price was $9,000. It was a 118 horsepower four wheel drive. Do you know what it would cost to buy that today? It would cost $65,000. In 1967 I was getting $2.25 for a bushel of wheat. Today I am getting $4. The cost to increase my horsepower rose from $9,000 to $65,000. I see that my time is up. I hope the Minister understands the problem of the farming areas in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I will just make a few points to put our position about the Bill clearly on the record. I think the amendments improve the Bill. We lament the fact that we were not given more time in committee to make more improvements to the Bill. As the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) said, we served notice that there were other things to be done to the Bill which could have been done.
The comment which needs to be made is that it is too bad the Government did not have a Minister in the House to deal with the Bill. I think that would have made a difference. I would like to defend the Senate before I say what I am going to say. I think there are some excellent Senators and they do some excellent committee work. However, I have heard the Senate defined on occasion as living proof of life after death. If you look at the way in which the Minister who was responsible for this Bill performed on this Bill, it may put a little credence in that definition of the Senate. I say that just to make the point that I think we could have dealt more effectively with this Bill had we had someone in the House who was prepared to deal with it in a little more urgent and animated way. We probably would have had some better amendments.
We are happy to see the change in the trigger mechanism so that there will be a pay-out this year. In saying that, I would urge the Government again to give the Bill Royal Assent and
to get the arithmetic done so that we can have an interim payment which is as large as possible and as quickly as possible. That has been our concern since the start. We hope that the Government will take this as notice and get the payment out as quickly as possible.
We have some concerns about having it changed from a calendar year to a crop year basis. The jury is still out as to whether or not that will be an improvement. It is certainly a welcome improvement to allow spouses to be eligible to participate on a multiple basis. That is a worth-while improvement to the Bill and something which could have been done sooner. It is certainly welcome now.
With regard to the withdrawal procedure, I think it remains to be seen whether we need to go on a 10-year basis. I am not convinced that that could not be shortened. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talked about producers wanting to have the option to withdraw. I think that is a valid concern. Ten years seems excessively long to a lot of producers. I wonder how that is going to work. We basically support the amendments. The Government has caught us between a rock and a hard place by bringing it in at this late date in the session. We certainly have to give approval to the Bill but I would like to reiterate the fact that the improvements could have been substantially better in many ways and the legislation is still flawed. It is going to require improvements in the future. With that I will close by saying that we hope the Bill is given Royal Assent as quickly as possible and that the cash which is urgently needed will be in the producers' hands as quickly as possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order with reference to an incident which transpired earlier this evening. The Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) stood in his place and indicated to the House that there had been consultations and consent given with respect to reverting to Motions in order that a report from the finance committee could in fact be tabled. I have spoken directly to the Member for Willowdale about this matter indicating my displeasure with the step that was taken by him in indicating that he had consulted. He had in fact not consulted.
We try to operate this place on the basis of a person's word being taken for granted. I was out of the Chamber very briefly. I am sorry this has happened. I do not like to see this kind of a matter dealt with in this way. If there are going to be consultations I am pleased to have discussions. I am sure the matter could have been resolved. However, for the Member for Willowdale to come into the House and indicate that he had consulted with me is simply not the fact. I want to put that on
June 27, 1984

the record. If that happens again we are going to find ourselves in a position where we simply will not agree to anything except in the normal course of events. I think that would be a very unfortunate way to have to operate the House of Commons. We operate on the basis of consultation with the House Leaders. I would not presume, nor would any member of my caucus, to say that there had been consultations with the Government House Leader if there had not been. I would do him the courtesy of making sure that there was a clear understanding with respect to the matter. It is a fait accompli. I simply bring this to your attention because I am concerned about the activities that have taken place. I have said that I have spoken directly to the Member for Willowdale and indicated to him my intense displeasure with what has transpired today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, concerning what my colleague opposite just said, I was in the House when the Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) rose on a point of order. He did not mention consultation. He asked for unanimous consent, and I want to set the record straight. He only asked for unanimous consent to table the report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, in connection with Bill C-36. That is what he said in the House. In any case, my hon. friend will be able to check the record in Hansard tomorrow. He never mentioned consultation, he just asked for unanimous consent and that is when the Hon. Member's colleague behind him, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), rose and asked to see what it was. As far as I know, there never was any consultation. He just asked for, and obtained, the unanimous consent of the House to table this report.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On this point, whether or not there were consultations of course is not within the purview of the Chair. The Chair heard an Hon. Member asking for consent and the Chair asked whether there was consent in the House. It eventually became clear that consent was available. However, with regard to consultations, there is not much that I can do.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the observations with respect to this are very pertinent to the activity and the work we must do over the next two days. There was no question in my mind whatsoever that, implicit in the words of the Hon. Member, there would be agreement if you were to seek unanimous consent. I certainly would not have given unanimous consent until I was certain that there had been consultations, either with my House Leader or the finance spokesman for our Party. Indeed, I would not have risen had I not taken that inference. Of course I am imputing motives. There is no question about that. It is an unparliamentary thing for me to do and I very rarely do it. If I am, I will apologize. On the other hand, with any further occurrence of that kind, unless I
Committee Report
am absolutely satisfied that in the absence of my House Leader there has been consultation on concurrence, unfortunately there will not be consent given; not until such time as there is some assurance on all sides of the House.
The inference from the distinguished House Leader of the NDP, implicit in his question about why I was objecting, gave even further rise to my concern. There was no consultation and it was implicit in the seeking of consent.
In any event, I suspect that in the parliamentary process, with the courtesy that we follow, there is no attempt to seek unanimous consent without prior consultation in some usual or informal sense. You are nodding your head in the negative, Mr. Speaker. In the 19 or 20 years that I have been here there has always been the courtesy of consultation, conversation or discussion and then a process, unless in the usual way, the Government House Leader is attempting to further the Government's own ends. That was not the case this evening.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise very briefly. I understand that perhaps my hon. colleague has not witnessed in the past the seeking of unanimous consent without previous consultations having been held. I believe him. I have no reason to doubt his word that that never happened while he was physically sitting in the House. But he must have been away for many long periods of time. I have only been here ten years and during those ten years I very often have witnessed Members seeking unanimous consent without previous consultation.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Not so at all.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Probably my hon. colleague was campaigning for his nomination convention in Halifax, but that is understandable. However, that is the case.
What is clear now is that a colleague of mine was in the House when this happened. I see that the Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) is here and he will have an opportunity to clarify it. But we were told that he never indicated that previous consultations had been held. He was just merely seeking unanimous consent. I believe the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Dubois) has just indicated that. I was not in the House, but if the Opposition suspects that we wanted to play a trick on them, I can assure them that we will not deal with this Bill before the end of June without their consent. So they should be very at ease. We are very sincere and acting in good faith. What was done was done in the normal practice.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is not normal practice.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If my hon. colleague felt tricked, betrayed or that in his opinion the usual practice was not followed, he should rest at ease. We will not deal with the Bill before the end of June unless we have the unanimous consent of the House. I can give him that assurance.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Opposition is making a mountain of a mole hill. I was called to the Chamber, on a couple of minutes' notice in my capacity as chairman of the Finance Committee to table the Sixth Report of the

June 27, 1984
Committee Report
Finance Committee. It is a matter which had been discussed by all Parties this afternoon.
I came down in my capacity as chairman of the Finance Committee to do this and I sought the unanimous consent of the House. I explained the matter to the House. The Hon. Member opposite was shown the report, as was the House leader of the NDP, which we sought to table. I sought the unanimous consent of the House to revert to Tabling Reports from Standing and Special Committees.
What happened, unfortunately, is that the House Leader for the Opposition approached me outside the Chamber. I said yes, I understood that there was consent to table this particular report at that particular time. I never assured the Hon. House Leader for the Opposition that we had consent, I said that I understood that we had consent. For him to stand in the House and try to make it appear that I have deliberately tried to mislead the House bothers me a great deal.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: There weren't very many here but you sure as hell misled me.

I did not under any circumstances indicate, other than to the House Leader outside the Chamber, that I
had understood that consent had been obtained to do this tabling at that particular time. There was no attempt to mislead Hon. Members opposite. I do not see how there can be any complaint in terms of what our House Leader has said, that nothing will be done with respect to this Report without the unanimous consent of the Chamber. I do not know how our House Leader could be more fair. I do not know how the House Leader of the Opposition could have been more misleading in terms of what I had said to him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that if I have ever heard an admission of guilt from any member, it came out of the mouth of the Member of Willowdale (Mr. Peterson). I simply do not think we can take his word with respect to matters in the future.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hansard will speak for itself tomorrow.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
